nehemiah-1:1:1.summary: “Neemias son of Achalia” appears again at the head of those sealing the covenant.

nehemiah-1:1:0.summary: Both date events to the month “Chaseleu/Chaseelou,” but the years and events differ.
nehemiah-1:1:0.why: Identifies the month as the ninth.
nehemiah-1:1:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

nehemiah-1:1:2.summary: Nehemiah’s “Sousan” is Susa, where Artaxerxes was enthroned.

nehemiah-1:1:3.summary: Nehemiah’s “Sousan abira” is the city of Susa where Daniel saw his vision.
nehemiah-1:1:3.why: Earlier significance of the same city.

nehemiah-1:1:4.summary: Ezra’s return under Arthasastha precedes Nehemiah’s twentieth year, but no date is shared.
nehemiah-1:1:4.why: Chronological background on the same reign.

nehemiah-1:1:5.summary: Both mention Susa, but Esther’s event is unrelated to Nehemiah.

nehemiah-1:1:6.summary: The narrative continues “in the twentieth year” of King Arthasastha, matching the source’s dating.
nehemiah-1:1:6.why: Gives the king and continuation of the story.

nehemiah-1:1:7.summary: Ezra 10:9 dates an event to the ninth month (Chaseelou’s position), but the shown text lacks the name.

nehemiah-1:2:0.summary: Nehemiah’s brother “Anani” is likely the brother “Anania” later put in charge in Jerusalem.

nehemiah-1:2:1.summary: Both speak of survivors from captivity, but Ezekiel addresses repentance among the nations.

nehemiah-1:2:2.summary: Both mention survivors, but Ezekiel speaks of judgment, not the returned remnant.

nehemiah-1:2:3.summary: Ezra praises God for “leaving some of us for deliverance” and a fence in Judah and Jerusalem, matching the remnant Nehemiah asks about.
nehemiah-1:2:3.why: Shows the remnant’s condition from Ezra’s perspective.

nehemiah-1:2:4.summary: Both involve a survivor bringing news of Jerusalem, but the settings differ.
nehemiah-1:2:4.why: Loose parallel of reports reaching exiles.

nehemiah-1:2:5.summary: Both show concern for Jerusalem, the psalm urging prayer for its peace.

nehemiah-1:2:6.summary: Ezra fears no “remnant or survivor” will remain, loosely paralleling Nehemiah’s question about survivors.

nehemiah-1:2:7.summary: Jeremiah speaks of Judah’s remainder in Egypt not being saved, a loose remnant parallel.

nehemiah-1:2:8.summary: The exile’s vow to remember Jerusalem loosely parallels Nehemiah’s concern for Jerusalem.

nehemiah-1:3:0.summary: Nehemiah later repeats the report: “distress,” Jerusalem’s “gates have been given to fire,” and “a disgrace.”
nehemiah-1:3:0.why: Shows Nehemiah acting on the report.

nehemiah-1:3:1.summary: The shown text, “the chief cook,” contains nothing about Jerusalem’s walls.

nehemiah-1:3:2.summary: Ezra 5:8 reports temple building progress, not ruined walls and burned gates.
nehemiah-1:3:2.why: No real link in the texts shown.

nehemiah-1:3:3.summary: Nehemiah tells the king the city is laid waste and “its gates have been consumed by fire.”
nehemiah-1:3:3.why: Shows Nehemiah relaying the report to the king.

nehemiah-1:3:4.summary: Nehemiah inspects the wall “they were pulling down” and gates “consumed by fire.”
nehemiah-1:3:4.why: Shows Nehemiah seeing the reported damage.

nehemiah-1:3:5.summary: Both mention the people being “in great distress,” in different contexts.
nehemiah-1:3:5.why: Shared phrase about the remnant’s hardship.

nehemiah-1:3:6.summary: Both concern those who came up “from the captivity” to Judah, but the lists add little here.

nehemiah-1:3:7.summary: Both speak of Jerusalem’s reproach, but Jeremiah warns those going to Egypt.

nehemiah-1:3:8.summary: Isaiah foresees an abandoned city, a general parallel to Jerusalem’s ruin; truncated range.

nehemiah-1:3:9.summary: Lamentations mentions “reproach,” a general parallel to the remnant’s disgrace.

nehemiah-1:3:10.summary: Lamentations asks God to “see our reproach,” a general parallel to the remnant’s disgrace.

nehemiah-1:3:11.summary: “We became a reproach to our neighbors” loosely parallels the remnant’s disgrace.

nehemiah-1:3:12.summary: Isaiah laments Jerusalem become a desert and the holy house “fire-burned,” matching burned gates and ruined city.

nehemiah-1:3:13.summary: Jeremiah speaks of becoming a “reproach” but addresses survivors in Egypt; truncated range.

nehemiah-1:3:14.summary: God gave Israel “to reproach,” loosely paralleling the remnant’s disgrace.

nehemiah-1:3:17.summary: Both concern those who came up from the captivity, but the list adds little here.

nehemiah-1:3:18.summary: The Chaldeans “pulled down the whole wall of Jerusalem,” the destruction the report describes.
nehemiah-1:3:18.why: Explains how the walls were pulled down.

nehemiah-1:3:19.summary: The command to tear down battlements loosely parallels Jerusalem’s pulled-down walls.
nehemiah-1:3:19.why: Prophetic threat of the walls’ ruin.

nehemiah-1:3:20.summary: Israel made “a reproach to our neighbors” loosely parallels the remnant’s disgrace.

nehemiah-1:3:21.summary: The exiles weeping in Babylon loosely parallels grief over Jerusalem’s state.

nehemiah-1:3:22.summary: Warning that Israel would become a byword loosely parallels the remnant’s disgrace.

nehemiah-1:3:23.summary: Jeremiah foresees Judah as “a reproach,” loosely parallel to the remnant’s disgrace.

nehemiah-1:3:24.summary: Mordecai’s dream shares nothing specific with the report about Jerusalem’s walls.
nehemiah-1:3:24.why: No real link in the texts shown.

nehemiah-1:3:25.summary: Jerusalem remembering her humiliation loosely parallels the remnant’s distress.

nehemiah-1:3:26.summary: Both speak of people in “the country,” but Nehemiah 11:3 lists settlers, not distress.

nehemiah-1:3:27.summary: God threatens to “pull down its wall,” loosely paralleling Jerusalem’s pulled-down walls.

nehemiah-1:3:28.summary: Judas finds “the gates burned down” in a later desolation, a similar image of a different event.
nehemiah-1:3:28.why: Similar scene of ruin centuries later.

nehemiah-1:4:1.summary: Both “sat” and “wept” over Zion/Jerusalem from exile.

nehemiah-1:4:2.summary: Ezra likewise prays, confesses and weeps over the people’s plight.
nehemiah-1:4:2.why: Parallel response of a returning leader.

nehemiah-1:4:3.summary: The psalmist’s fasting from zeal for God’s house loosely parallels Nehemiah’s fasting.

nehemiah-1:4:4.summary: Compassion for Zion’s stones and dust loosely parallels Nehemiah’s grief for Jerusalem.

nehemiah-1:4:5.summary: Nehemiah again “prayed to the God of heaven” before answering the king.

nehemiah-1:4:6.summary: God promises to gather the crushed and asks who took up reproach, a loose parallel.

nehemiah-1:4:7.summary: “Weep with those who weep” loosely parallels Nehemiah’s weeping for his people.

nehemiah-1:4:8.summary: Daniel calls for “fasting and supplication” in crisis, loosely parallel to Nehemiah’s fasting prayer.

nehemiah-1:4:9.summary: Jonah calls God “the God of heaven,” the same title Nehemiah uses.

nehemiah-1:4:10.summary: The returned exiles call themselves slaves of “the God of heaven,” the title Nehemiah uses.
nehemiah-1:4:10.why: Shared divine title in the return era.

nehemiah-1:4:11.summary: Ezra too reacts: “When I heard this word,” mourned and “sat,” paralleling Nehemiah’s response.
nehemiah-1:4:11.why: Parallel mourning response of a leader.

nehemiah-1:4:12.summary: Eli’s household reacts with grief to disastrous news, a loose parallel; truncated range.

nehemiah-1:5:0.summary: Nehemiah’s “mercy for those who love Him and keep His commandments” echoes the Decalogue’s promise.
nehemiah-1:5:0.why: Shows the covenant formula Nehemiah quotes.

nehemiah-1:5:2.summary: Deuteronomy calls the Lord “a great and mighty God,” matching Nehemiah’s address.
nehemiah-1:5:2.why: Shows the source of Nehemiah’s titles.

nehemiah-1:5:4.summary: Nehemiah later urges the people to remember “our God, great and fearsome.”
nehemiah-1:5:4.why: Same description used in Nehemiah’s crisis.

nehemiah-1:5:5.summary: The later prayer repeats “mighty, great... fearsome One, who dost keep Thy covenant and Thy mercy.”
nehemiah-1:5:5.why: Same covenant formula repeated in prayer.

nehemiah-1:5:6.summary: Solomon also addresses God as “keeping covenant and mercy” in prayer.
nehemiah-1:5:6.why: Same covenant formula in Solomon’s prayer.

nehemiah-1:5:7.summary: Hebrews stresses God’s faithfulness to His promise, a general parallel to covenant-keeping; truncated range.

nehemiah-1:5:8.summary: God making Himself “a great and manifest name” loosely relates to Nehemiah’s “Great” God.

nehemiah-1:5:9.summary: The psalm calls the Lord “fearsome, a great King,” matching Nehemiah’s “Great and Fearsome.”

nehemiah-1:6:0.summary: Daniel likewise prays “confessing my sins and the sins of my people Israel.”

nehemiah-1:6:1.summary: Daniel’s prayer opens with nearly identical words: “great, strong, and fearsome God, keeping the covenant and mercy.”

nehemiah-1:6:2.summary: The Lord’s “eyes” and “ears toward their supplication” match Nehemiah’s plea for attentive ears and open eyes.
nehemiah-1:6:2.why: Grounds the plea in God’s attentiveness.

nehemiah-1:6:3.summary: “We sinned with our fathers” matches Nehemiah’s confession, “I and my father’s house have sinned.”

nehemiah-1:6:4.summary: Daniel asks God to “hear Thy servant’s prayer,” “Attend with Thine ear” and “Open Thine eyes.”

nehemiah-1:6:5.summary: Hezekiah confesses that “our fathers” did evil, a general parallel to ancestral sin.

nehemiah-1:6:7.summary: Isaiah confesses his own and his people’s uncleanness, loosely parallel to Nehemiah’s confession.

nehemiah-1:6:8.summary: “If we confess our sins” relates generally to Nehemiah’s confession.

nehemiah-1:6:9.summary: Crying to God “day and night” loosely parallels Nehemiah’s day-and-night prayer.

nehemiah-1:6:10.summary: Paul’s petitions “night and day” loosely parallel Nehemiah’s continual prayer.

nehemiah-1:6:11.summary: “Our fathers sinned” relates generally to Nehemiah’s confession of his father’s house.

nehemiah-1:6:12.summary: “We have sinned and acted godlessly” relates generally to Nehemiah’s confession.

nehemiah-1:6:13.summary: Isaiah’s confession of the people’s uncleanness and sins loosely parallels Nehemiah’s.

nehemiah-1:6:14.summary: Solomon prays that God’s “eyes may be open” to hear His servant’s prayer “day and night.”

nehemiah-1:6:15.summary: The psalmist confesses his sin to the Lord, a general parallel to Nehemiah’s confession.

nehemiah-1:6:16.summary: “Let Thine ears be attentive” matches Nehemiah’s “let Thine ear be attentive.”

nehemiah-1:6:17.summary: Praying evening, morning and noon loosely parallels Nehemiah’s day-and-night prayer.

nehemiah-1:6:19.summary: Ezra likewise “prayed and confessed” for the people’s sins.
nehemiah-1:6:19.why: Parallel confession by a return-era leader.

nehemiah-1:6:20.summary: The widow’s prayers “night and day” loosely parallel Nehemiah’s continual prayer.

nehemiah-1:6:21.summary: Paul includes himself among sinners, loosely parallel to Nehemiah’s “I... have sinned.”

nehemiah-1:6:22.summary: Crying out “by day” and “by night” loosely parallels Nehemiah’s continual prayer.

nehemiah-1:6:23.summary: Ezra’s call to “give praise” and separate does not carry a confession link in the shown wording.
nehemiah-1:6:23.why: Shown wording lacks the confession link.

nehemiah-1:6:24.summary: Anna serves with “petitions night and day,” loosely parallel to Nehemiah’s continual prayer.

nehemiah-1:6:25.summary: Samuel cried to the Lord all night, loosely parallel to Nehemiah’s night prayer.

nehemiah-1:6:26.summary: The shown text speaks of bearing witness, not confessing sins against the Lord.
nehemiah-1:6:26.why: Shown wording lacks the confession link.

nehemiah-1:7:0.summary: Daniel confesses Israel “transgressed Thy commandments and judgments,” matching Nehemiah’s confession.

nehemiah-1:7:1.summary: Daniel confesses Israel abandoned the law “of Moses, God’s servant,” matching Nehemiah’s “Moses Thy servant.”

nehemiah-1:7:2.summary: Daniel ties Israel’s calamities to disobeying “Moses’ covenant,” paralleling Nehemiah’s confession.

nehemiah-1:7:3.summary: “We sinned with our fathers” relates generally to breaking faith with God.

nehemiah-1:7:4.summary: God’s call to accept discipline loosely relates to Israel’s unfaithfulness.

nehemiah-1:7:5.summary: The psalm uses “ordinances,” “commandments” and “judgments,” the same triad, but expresses desire to keep them.

nehemiah-1:7:7.summary: “The law of Moses My servant... ordinances and judgments” closely matches Nehemiah’s phrasing.
nehemiah-1:7:7.why: Same summary of the Mosaic law.

nehemiah-1:7:8.summary: “The commandments, and the ordinances, and the judgments which the Lord... commanded” matches Nehemiah’s list.
nehemiah-1:7:8.why: Shows the source of Nehemiah’s legal triad.

nehemiah-1:7:9.summary: Amaziah acted according to the law as commanded; only general reference to Moses’ law.

nehemiah-1:7:10.summary: The psalm praises the Lord’s ordinances, commandment and judgments, the same vocabulary in praise.

nehemiah-1:7:11.summary: “The commandments that the Lord commanded Moses” matches the commands given to “Moses Thy servant.”

nehemiah-1:7:12.summary: Moses proclaims “the ordinances and the judgments,” the commands Nehemiah says Israel did not keep.
nehemiah-1:7:12.why: Shows the commands given through Moses.

nehemiah-1:7:13.summary: Revelation praises God’s true judgments on Babylon, unrelated to Israel’s broken commandments.

nehemiah-1:7:14.summary: Moses taught “ordinances and judgments, as the Lord commanded me,” the commands Nehemiah cites.
nehemiah-1:7:14.why: Shows the commands given through Moses.

nehemiah-1:7:15.summary: The people “becoming corrupt” under Jotham does not carry Nehemiah’s wording “broken faith.”
nehemiah-1:7:15.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

nehemiah-1:7:16.summary: David charges Solomon to keep “commandments, statutes, and judgments written in Moses’ law.”

nehemiah-1:7:17.summary: Hosea’s “corrupted” does not match Nehemiah’s “broken faith” in the shown wording.
nehemiah-1:7:17.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

nehemiah-1:7:18.summary: Ezra is skilled in “the law of Moses,” loosely related to the commandments given to Moses.

nehemiah-1:7:19.summary: Moses tells Israel to “hear the ordinances and the judgments,” the commands Nehemiah confesses were not kept.
nehemiah-1:7:19.why: Shows the commands given through Moses.

nehemiah-1:7:20.summary: The later confession says Israel “sinned against Thy commandments and judgments,” echoing Nehemiah’s confession; truncated range.
nehemiah-1:7:20.why: Same confession repeated in national prayer.

nehemiah-1:8:1.summary: Moses warned that for lawlessness “the Lord shall scatter you among all the nations,” the word Nehemiah recalls.

nehemiah-1:8:3.summary: God warns that if Israel does not keep the commandments “Moses set before you,” He will remove Israel from the land.
nehemiah-1:8:3.why: Another form of the covenant warning.

nehemiah-1:8:4.summary: God says, “I will scatter them,” the threat Nehemiah recalls as Moses’ word.
nehemiah-1:8:4.why: Shows the scattering threat in Moses’ song.

nehemiah-1:8:5.summary: God remembering “His holy covenant” loosely parallels Nehemiah’s appeal to God’s word.

nehemiah-1:8:6.summary: “Remember Thy word to Thy servant” closely matches Nehemiah’s “Remember... the word.”

nehemiah-1:9:0.summary: God promises to be found when sought, loosely parallel to the promise for those who return.

nehemiah-1:9:2.summary: Moses foresaw that in distress “you shall return unto the Lord your God,” the promise Nehemiah recalls.
nehemiah-1:9:2.why: Shows the restoration promise Nehemiah cites.

nehemiah-1:9:3.summary: God promises: “I am gathering them from all the land where I scattered them” and bringing them back.

nehemiah-1:9:4.summary: Leviticus promises that if the scattered confess their sins, God will remember His covenant.
nehemiah-1:9:4.why: Background to the repentance and return promise.

nehemiah-1:9:5.summary: The Lord “will gather the dispersed of Israel,” matching “your dispersed people... I will gather them.”
nehemiah-1:9:5.why: Same promise of gathering the dispersed.

nehemiah-1:9:6.summary: Gathering His chosen “from one end of the heavens to the other” echoes gathering from “the farthest edge of heaven.”
nehemiah-1:9:6.why: New Testament echo of the gathering image.

nehemiah-1:9:8.summary: The Lord “who gathers Israel’s scattered people” matches the promise to gather the dispersed.

nehemiah-1:9:9.summary: “The God whose name dwells there” matches “the place I chose for My name to dwell.”
nehemiah-1:9:9.why: Shows the temple as the chosen place.

nehemiah-1:9:10.summary: God promises to return and settle the scattered in their land, a general restoration parallel.

nehemiah-1:9:11.summary: “Gather you out of all the lands and bring you into your own land” matches the promise to gather and bring them.

nehemiah-1:9:12.summary: God will “gather Judah’s scattered ones from the earth’s four wings,” paralleling gathering from the farthest edge.

nehemiah-1:9:13.summary: The prayer “gather us together from the nations” asks for the gathering Nehemiah recalls.

nehemiah-1:9:14.summary: God promises to restore Israel to his pasture, a general restoration parallel.

nehemiah-1:9:15.summary: God consecrated the house “to put My name there,” the place chosen for His name.

nehemiah-1:9:16.summary: “He who winnowed Israel will gather him” matches the promise to gather the dispersed.

nehemiah-1:9:17.summary: “Return... and bring you into Zion” parallels turning back and being brought to the chosen place.
nehemiah-1:9:17.why: Same call to return and promise.

nehemiah-1:9:18.summary: “Rescue us from the nations” loosely parallels the hope of gathering from dispersion.

nehemiah-1:9:19.summary: “The place which the Lord your God shall choose for His name” matches Nehemiah’s phrasing.
nehemiah-1:9:19.why: Shows the Deuteronomic source of the phrase.

nehemiah-1:10:0.summary: “These are Thy people... by Thy great strength” closely matches Nehemiah’s plea.
nehemiah-1:10:0.why: Same appeal Moses made for Israel.

nehemiah-1:10:1.summary: Daniel recalls God bringing “Thy people out of Egypt with Thine uplifted arm,” as Nehemiah does; truncated range.

nehemiah-1:10:2.summary: Moses pleads for “Thy people” led out “with great strength,” matching Nehemiah’s appeal.

nehemiah-1:10:3.summary: Isaiah appeals to God for “Thy servants” and inheritance, a general parallel.

nehemiah-1:10:4.summary: “With a mighty hand” describes the Exodus deliverance Nehemiah recalls.

nehemiah-1:10:5.summary: “The Lord your God redeemed you” shares the redemption idea but not the hand and power language.

nehemiah-1:10:6.summary: “This people of Thine whom Thou didst redeem... in Thy strength” matches Nehemiah’s description.

nehemiah-1:10:7.summary: “With a mighty hand the Lord God brought you out” matches Nehemiah’s “mighty hand.”

nehemiah-1:10:8.summary: God promises deliverance “with a mighty hand” and an uplifted arm.

nehemiah-1:10:9.summary: “We are all Thy people” loosely parallels “They are... Thy people.”

nehemiah-1:10:10.summary: God “didst redeem” His inheritance, loosely parallel to redeeming His people.

nehemiah-1:11:0.summary: Nehemiah repeats his opening plea: “let Thine ear be attentive... to hear Thy servant’s prayer.”

nehemiah-1:11:2.summary: “A king’s heart in God’s hand” explains Nehemiah’s plea for compassion before the king.
nehemiah-1:11:2.why: Grounds trust that God moves kings.

nehemiah-1:11:3.summary: Nehemiah, “the king’s cupbearer,” serves the king wine as the story resumes.
nehemiah-1:11:3.why: Shows the cupbearer’s role in the next scene.

nehemiah-1:11:4.summary: A request for prayer by those wishing to act well loosely parallels those who “wish to fear Thy name.”

nehemiah-1:11:5.summary: “The king granted him his requests” because God’s hand was on Ezra, paralleling Nehemiah’s plea for favor.
nehemiah-1:11:5.why: Shows God granting favor with the king.

nehemiah-1:11:6.summary: “Let Thine ears be attentive” matches Nehemiah’s “let Thine ear be attentive.”

nehemiah-1:11:7.summary: “Give ear, Lord, to my prayer” closely parallels Nehemiah’s plea.

nehemiah-1:11:9.summary: Both mention a royal cupbearer, but Pharaoh’s cupbearer is unrelated.

nehemiah-1:11:10.summary: God stirring Cyrus’s spirit loosely parallels Nehemiah’s plea for favor with a king.

nehemiah-1:11:11.summary: Pharaoh’s cupbearer is unrelated beyond the shared office.

nehemiah-1:11:12.summary: Hoping in God’s name loosely parallels those who “wish to fear Thy name.”

nehemiah-1:11:13.summary: Pharaoh’s cupbearer serving the cup is unrelated beyond the shared office; truncated range.

nehemiah-1:11:14.summary: Jacob’s plea for deliverance before meeting Esau loosely parallels a plea before facing a powerful man.
nehemiah-1:11:14.why: Loose parallel of prayer before a meeting.

nehemiah-1:11:15.summary: Pharaoh’s cupbearer is unrelated beyond the shared office.

nehemiah-1:11:16.summary: “May my God give you grace before the man” closely parallels “give him compassion before this man.”
nehemiah-1:11:16.why: Similar prayer for favor before a ruler.

nehemiah-1:11:17.summary: Jacob’s renaming shares nothing specific with Nehemiah’s prayer.
nehemiah-1:11:17.why: No real link in the texts shown.

nehemiah-1:11:18.summary: Those who “did not choose the fear of the Lord” contrast with those who wish to fear His name.

nehemiah-1:11:19.summary: Pharaoh’s cupbearer is unrelated beyond the shared office.

nehemiah-1:3:15.summary: Jeremiah 29:18 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
nehemiah-1:3:15.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
nehemiah-1:3:15.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

nehemiah-1:3:16.summary: Jeremiah 39:8 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
nehemiah-1:3:16.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
nehemiah-1:3:16.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

nehemiah-2:1:0.summary: Esdras goes up in the reign of Arthasastha, the same Persian king Nehemiah serves.
nehemiah-2:1:0.why: Places Ezra and Nehemiah under the same king.

nehemiah-2:1:2.summary: The same “twentieth year” opens Nehemiah's account in Chaseelou, months before Nisan.
nehemiah-2:1:2.why: Links the dating of chapters 1 and 2.

nehemiah-2:1:3.summary: Ezra's return is dated by Arthasastha's reign, the same king.

nehemiah-2:1:4.summary: Esther dates events by Artaxerxes's regnal year and months at the Persian court; the link is only chronological style.

nehemiah-2:1:5.summary: The restored cupbearer gives the cup into Pharaoh's hand, as Nehemiah gives the king wine.
nehemiah-2:1:5.why: Parallel image of a cupbearer serving a foreign king.

nehemiah-2:1:6.summary: The cupbearer gives the cup into Pharaoh's hands, a parallel to Nehemiah serving wine.

nehemiah-2:2:0.summary: A sorrowful heart makes the face gloomy, matching the king's reading of Nehemiah's face.

nehemiah-2:2:1.summary: Joseph asks “Why are your faces downcast?” as the king asks why Nehemiah's face is distressed.
nehemiah-2:2:1.why: Parallel court question about a sad face.

nehemiah-2:3:1.summary: Bathsheba says “May my lord King David live for ever!” the same court formula.

nehemiah-2:3:2.summary: The shown verse only introduces Daniel; it lacks the “live for ever” greeting.

nehemiah-2:3:3.summary: The Chaldeans say “My lord king, live for ever!” the same royal greeting.

nehemiah-2:3:4.summary: Remembering Jerusalem above all joy parallels Nehemiah's grief for the city.

nehemiah-2:3:5.summary: Hezekiah buried at the tombs of David's sons, loosely related to “my fathers’ tombs” in Jerusalem.
nehemiah-2:3:5.why: Background on royal tombs in Jerusalem.

nehemiah-2:3:6.summary: Mentions burial in David's city and kings' tombs, loosely related to Nehemiah's ancestral tombs.

nehemiah-2:3:7.summary: Jerusalem's gates destroyed and fixed in the earth parallel the burned gates Nehemiah mourns.
nehemiah-2:3:7.why: Earlier lament over the city's gates.

nehemiah-2:3:8.summary: Daniel's “O king, I am still alive” in this text does not carry the “live for ever” greeting.
nehemiah-2:3:8.why: The Greek wording lacks the formula.

nehemiah-2:3:9.summary: Mentions burial in David's city but not the kings' tombs; only loose link to ancestral tombs.

nehemiah-2:3:10.summary: The shown verse only says the men approached the king, without the greeting.

nehemiah-2:3:11.summary: God's servants pity Zion's stones and dust, like Nehemiah's grief over ruined Jerusalem.
nehemiah-2:3:11.why: Shared longing for the ruined city.

nehemiah-2:3:12.summary: “My lord king, live for ever!” is the same court greeting.

nehemiah-2:4:0.summary: Making requests known to God in prayer parallels Nehemiah praying before answering the king.

nehemiah-2:4:1.summary: Acknowledging wisdom in all ways is only generally like Nehemiah turning to God.

nehemiah-2:4:2.summary: Nehemiah prayed “before the God of heaven” earlier, the same address used here.

nehemiah-2:4:4.summary: God asks Solomon to make a request, similar in form to the king's question.

nehemiah-2:4:5.summary: Jesus asks “What do you want?” as the king asks Nehemiah his request.

nehemiah-2:4:6.summary: The Persian king asks Esther what she wants, inviting a request as Arthasastha does.

nehemiah-2:4:7.summary: The king asks Esther her petition and request, like the king's question to Nehemiah.

nehemiah-3:15:12.summary: The king's garden near the walls may relate to the king's pool, but it is not named.

nehemiah-3:15:13.summary: Mizpah is not named in the Saints text of this verse.

nehemiah-3:17:3.summary: Levite supervisors over the works loosely parallel Levites repairing.

nehemiah-3:22:1.summary: The plain of Ono shares nothing with the transliterated Achechar.
nehemiah-3:22:1.why: No link in the shown text.

nehemiah-3:23:0.summary: Repaired “opposite his house,” the same practice.

nehemiah-3:23:1.summary: The shown verse names Jesus, Banaias and Sarabia; no builder named here.

nehemiah-3:23:2.summary: Ananias and Maasaia appear, matching Azaria's ancestors' names, but identity is uncertain.

nehemiah-3:23:4.summary: A priest Azaria signs the covenant; identity with the builder is uncertain.

nehemiah-3:24:2.summary: Another “second section” in the same list.

nehemiah-3:24:3.summary: Another “second” section in the same list.

nehemiah-3:25:1.summary: Jeremiah remains in the prison court, likely the court of the guard by the king's house.
nehemiah-3:25:1.why: Identifies the court of the guard.

nehemiah-3:25:2.summary: The Gate of the Guard is named on the dedication route.

nehemiah-3:25:3.summary: The sons of Phoros are Phadaia's clan.

nehemiah-3:25:4.summary: Jeremiah was bound in the prison court, likely the same court of the guard.

nehemiah-3:25:5.summary: Phadaias stands beside Esdras; identity with Phadaia is uncertain.

nehemiah-3:25:6.summary: The sons of Phoros appear in the census.

nehemiah-3:25:7.summary: A king's elaborate house loosely relates to the king's house named here.

nehemiah-3:25:8.summary: Jeremiah is taken from the prison court, likely the court of the guard.

nehemiah-3:26:0.summary: The people gather before the Water Gate to hear the law.
nehemiah-3:26:0.why: Same gate in a key later event.

nehemiah-3:26:2.summary: Continues the reading at the Water Gate, but the shown verse does not name it.
nehemiah-3:26:2.why: Same scene, gate not named here.

nehemiah-3:26:4.summary: Manasseh builds a wall toward Ophla, the area where the Nathinim lived.

nehemiah-3:26:5.summary: Jotham builds on the wall of Ophla.

nehemiah-3:26:6.summary: “The given ones” are the Nathinim living in the cities.

nehemiah-3:26:7.summary: Lists the families of the Nathinim.

nehemiah-3:26:8.summary: Shelters built in squares and by the Ephraim Gate; the Water Gate is not named here.

nehemiah-3:26:10.summary: The great projecting tower and the Ophla wall are named in the next section.

nehemiah-3:26:11.summary: Lists the families of the Nathinaians.

nehemiah-3:28:1.summary: The Gate of the Horsemen at the king's house is likely the Horse Gate.

nehemiah-3:28:2.summary: The horses' entrance of the king's house is likely the Horse Gate.

nehemiah-3:28:3.summary: Repaired “opposite his house,” the same practice.

nehemiah-3:28:4.summary: Repaired “opposite their house,” the same practice.

nehemiah-3:29:0.summary: Sechenias son of Iiel is a different man from Samaia's father Sechenia.

nehemiah-3:29:1.summary: The sons of Emmer are Saddouk's family.

nehemiah-3:29:2.summary: The sons of Emmer appear in Ezra's list.

nehemiah-3:29:3.summary: The Charsith Gate is not the East Gate named here.

nehemiah-3:31:0.summary: The “dealers in small wares” continue to the Sheep Gate.
nehemiah-3:31:0.why: Same tradesmen in the next section.

nehemiah-3:31:1.summary: Another entry in the same repair list; no trade named in the Saints text.

nehemiah-3:32:1.summary: The Sheep Gate in Jerusalem appears in John.

nehemiah-3:32:2.summary: The Sheep Gate is on the dedication route.

nehemiah-3:32:3.summary: Another entry in the same repair list.

nehemiah-3:32:4.summary: The “dealers in small wares” are named in both verses.

nehemiah-3:33:0.summary: Sanaballat hears, and it “displeased” him, as before.

nehemiah-3:33:1.summary: The faithful experienced mockery, a general parallel.

nehemiah-3:33:2.summary: Enemies mocked the psalmist, a general parallel.

nehemiah-3:33:3.summary: Leaders filled with jealousy oppose God's work, a general parallel.

nehemiah-3:33:5.summary: Soldiers mock Jesus as “King of the Jews,” a general parallel.

nehemiah-3:33:6.summary: Israel made scorn and ridicule among neighbours.

nehemiah-3:33:7.summary: Enemies hear that Judah is building and oppose it.

nehemiah-3:34:0.summary: God uses the weak to shame the strong, a loose answer to the taunt.
nehemiah-3:34:0.why: Theological answer to mockery of weakness.

nehemiah-3:34:1.summary: Settlers in the cities of Somoron oppose Jerusalem's rebuilding.

nehemiah-3:34:2.summary: Goliath taunts David's weakness, loosely like Sanaballat's taunt.

nehemiah-3:34:3.summary: The weak made strong loosely answers the taunt about strength.
nehemiah-3:34:3.why: Promise of strength to the weak.

nehemiah-3:34:4.summary: Judah speaks of strength and doubts it can build; Saints reads the enemies' strength crushed.
nehemiah-3:34:4.why: Related talk of strength in building.

nehemiah-3:34:5.summary: The dry bones link rests on the Hebrew idea of reviving stones, absent in Saints.
nehemiah-3:34:5.why: The Greek-based wording lacks the link.

nehemiah-3:34:6.summary: Habakkuk's prayer has no specific link to the taunt.

nehemiah-3:34:7.summary: The wall's joyful dedication contrasts with the taunt, but the link is loose.

nehemiah-3:34:8.summary: Great sacrifices and gladness contrast with the mockery, but the link is loose.

nehemiah-3:34:9.summary: Philistines taunt the Hebrews, loosely like Sanaballat's scorn.

nehemiah-3:35:1.summary: Taking men alive has no link to the fox taunt.

nehemiah-3:35:2.summary: The Assyrian taunts Judah's weakness, loosely like the enemies' scorn.

nehemiah-3:35:3.summary: An enemy taunt mocks Samaria using “foxes,” like the fox jibe at the wall.

nehemiah-3:35:4.summary: Tobia the Ammoni joins Sanaballat in displeasure.

nehemiah-3:35:5.summary: Sanaballat and Tobia hear the wall is built.

nehemiah-3:35:6.summary: Foxes pass through ruined Zion, the image the enemies use in their taunt.
nehemiah-3:35:6.why: Gives weight to the fox image.

nehemiah-3:36:1.summary: The psalmist pleads for mercy because God's people are filled with contempt and reproach.

nehemiah-3:36:2.summary: The Lord opposes the proud, loosely like turning back the mockers.
nehemiah-3:36:2.why: General principle of God resisting scorners.

nehemiah-3:36:3.summary: The Lord will repay Ephraim's “reproach” upon him, like turning reproach back on their heads.

nehemiah-3:37:1.summary: Prays that lawlessness be remembered and sin “not be erased,” like “do not cover over lawlessness.”

nehemiah-3:37:2.summary: Asks God to add lawlessness to their lawlessness and not erase it for them.

nehemiah-3:37:3.summary: God wipes away lawless acts, the opposite of what Nehemiah asks for enemies.

nehemiah-3:37:4.summary: The Lord will repay Alexander, a general parallel to asking God to judge.

nehemiah-3:37:5.summary: God wipes out lawless acts, opposite to Nehemiah's plea.

nehemiah-3:37:6.summary: A plea to blot out one's own lawless deed contrasts with not covering the enemies'.

nehemiah-3:37:7.summary: “Blot out all my lawless deeds” is the opposite request.

nehemiah-3:37:8.summary: “Have no compassion on any who work lawlessness” matches the plea not to cover lawlessness.

nehemiah-3:37:9.summary: Enemies taunt the people on the wall, loosely like the scorn of Nehemiah's foes.
nehemiah-3:37:9.why: Earlier enemy taunt at Jerusalem's wall.
