nehemiah-4:1:0.summary: Sanaballat again hears of the wall-building and is angered, the same opposition reported in the preceding verse.
nehemiah-4:1:0.why: Shows the opposition building up across the narrative.

nehemiah-4:1:1.summary: Sanaballat and Tobia “heard” and it “displeased” them, the first report of the same opponents’ hostility.
nehemiah-4:1:1.why: Introduces the same enemies and their motive.

nehemiah-4:1:2.summary: The devil’s fury against the woman has no specific link to Sanaballat’s anger over Jerusalem’s walls.
nehemiah-4:1:2.why: Only a generic idea of hostile rage.

nehemiah-4:1:3.summary: Opponents “heard” and were enraged, a loose parallel to the enemies’ reaction on hearing of the work.
nehemiah-4:1:3.why: General pattern of hostile reaction to God’s work.

nehemiah-4:1:4.summary: Names the sons of Ammon and their aggression, but no link to the wall or the Persian-era opponents.

nehemiah-4:1:5.summary: Authorities try to stop the apostles’ work with threats; only a general theme of opposing God’s work.
nehemiah-4:1:5.why: Loose theme of hindering God’s work.

nehemiah-4:1:6.summary: The dragon’s war on the woman’s offspring has no specific tie to the Ammanites and Arabs opposing the wall.

nehemiah-4:1:7.summary: Lists Ashdod and Philistine cities, but the Saints text of the source names no Ashdodites, only Arabs and Ammanites.
nehemiah-4:1:7.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.

nehemiah-4:1:8.summary: Oracle against Gaza, Ashkelon and Azotus; the source in this reading does not mention Azotus.
nehemiah-4:1:8.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.

nehemiah-4:1:9.summary: Nehemiah later finds Jews married to Ammanite and Azotian wives; the shared element is only these neighbouring peoples.
nehemiah-4:1:9.why: Shows later entanglement with the same peoples.

nehemiah-4:1:10.summary: Ammon’s sons rejoiced over Judah’s devastation, echoing Ammanite displeasure at Jerusalem’s restoration, but on a different occasion.
nehemiah-4:1:10.why: Background to Ammonite ill will toward Jerusalem.

nehemiah-4:1:11.summary: The sons of Ammon oppress Israel in the judges’ period; only general Ammonite hostility is shared.

nehemiah-4:1:12.summary: Sanaballat, Tobia and Gesam the Arabi “heard” and opposed the rebuilding, the same coalition of opponents.
nehemiah-4:1:12.why: Earlier stage of the same opposition.

nehemiah-4:1:13.summary: Oracle against Azotus, Ascalon and Accaron; the source in this reading does not mention Azotus.
nehemiah-4:1:13.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.

nehemiah-4:1:14.summary: Jephthah disputes with the king of the sons of Ammon over land; only general Ammonite conflict is shared.

nehemiah-4:1:15.summary: The ark is taken to Ashdod, but Ashdod is not named in the Saints source verse.
nehemiah-4:1:15.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.

nehemiah-4:1:16.summary: A report that building, including walls, is advancing well, loosely like news that the walls were growing.
nehemiah-4:1:16.why: Shows how rebuilding progress was reported.

nehemiah-4:1:17.summary: Uzziah fights the Arabs and Azotus; only the Arab name overlaps with the source’s list of opponents.
nehemiah-4:1:17.why: Background on Arab neighbours of Judah.

nehemiah-4:1:18.summary: Ammonite leaders suspect and humiliate David’s envoys; only general Ammonite hostility is shared.

nehemiah-4:1:19.summary: Moab and the sons of Ammon come against Judah for war, a general precedent of Ammonite aggression.
nehemiah-4:1:19.why: Precedent of Ammonite attack on Judah.

nehemiah-4:1:20.summary: Ammonite raiders are sent against Judah; only the Ammonites as hostile neighbours are shared.

nehemiah-4:1:21.summary: The enmity between the serpent’s seed and the woman’s seed has no specific link to opposition to the wall.

nehemiah-4:1:22.summary: Nahash the Ammonite threatens disgrace on Israel; only Ammonite hostility is shared.

nehemiah-4:1:23.summary: The people of the land hinder Judah’s building and write against Jerusalem’s walls, the same kind of opposition to restoration.

nehemiah-4:1:24.summary: A summons to view oppression in Samaria; Ashdod-based link is not present in either Saints text.

nehemiah-4:2:0.summary: A coalition including Ammon “took counsel together” against God’s people, loosely matching enemies gathering against Jerusalem.
nehemiah-4:2:0.why: Pattern of allied nations plotting against Israel.

nehemiah-4:2:1.summary: Many gather around Jeremiah plotting to prevail against him; only a general theme of hostile gathering.
nehemiah-4:2:1.why: General theme of conspiracy against God’s servants.

nehemiah-4:2:2.summary: A conspiracy forms to kill Paul; only a general theme of enemies banding together.

nehemiah-4:2:3.summary: Rulers “gathered together” against the Lord, a general echo of enemies gathering against Jerusalem.
nehemiah-4:2:3.why: Frames opposition as rebellion against God.

nehemiah-4:2:4.summary: Nations are warned that their counsel will be scattered, a theme of failed hostile plans rather than gathering itself.
nehemiah-4:2:4.why: Anticipates God frustrating the enemies’ plan.

nehemiah-4:3:0.summary: A call to be watchful against the adversary, loosely echoing the posting of guards against enemies.

nehemiah-4:3:1.summary: Believers pray together when rulers gather against them, a general parallel to praying under threat.
nehemiah-4:3:1.why: Prayer in response to hostile threats.

nehemiah-4:3:2.summary: Call on God in affliction and He will rescue; a general theme of prayer in trouble.
nehemiah-4:3:2.why: General encouragement to pray in danger.

nehemiah-4:3:3.summary: Jesus prays after opponents’ anger, but the scenes share no specific element beyond prayer.

nehemiah-4:3:4.summary: “Keep watch and pray” pairs prayer with vigilance just as the builders prayed and stationed guards day and night.
nehemiah-4:3:4.why: Distinctive pairing of prayer and watchfulness.

nehemiah-4:3:5.summary: Stay awake and pray to escape coming things; a general pairing of vigilance and prayer.

nehemiah-4:3:6.summary: Jacob renamed Israel for being strong with God; no specific link to prayer and guarding.

nehemiah-4:3:7.summary: Hezekiah prays before the Lord against Sennacherib’s threats, a general parallel to praying against enemies.
nehemiah-4:3:7.why: Model of prayer under military threat.

nehemiah-4:3:8.summary: The psalmist cries to God “evening, morning and noon” against enemies, loosely echoing day-and-night prayer.

nehemiah-4:3:9.summary: Gives the enemies’ plan of a surprise attack that the prayer and guards were meant to meet.
nehemiah-4:3:9.why: Explains the threat being guarded against.

nehemiah-4:3:10.summary: Jacob prays for deliverance from Esau whom he fears, a general parallel to prayer under threat.
nehemiah-4:3:10.why: Prayer when facing a hostile force.

nehemiah-4:4:0.summary: Lists burden bearers and quarrymen; the Saints source speaks of the enemies’ strength, not burden bearers.
nehemiah-4:4:0.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.

nehemiah-4:4:1.summary: Nebuchadnezzar’s exhausted army at Tyre shares no specific element with Judah’s complaint about rubble.

nehemiah-4:4:2.summary: The spies say they will “not be able” to go up, a loose echo of “we will not be able to build.”

nehemiah-4:4:3.summary: A psalm of trust against sinners with bows has no specific link to Judah’s discouragement over rubble.

nehemiah-4:4:4.summary: The people say it is not time to rebuild the Lord’s house, a loose parallel to giving up on building.

nehemiah-4:4:5.summary: The spies turned away Israel’s hearts; only a general theme of discouragement is shared.

nehemiah-4:5:0.summary: Men lie in wait to kill Paul, a loose parallel to enemies planning to come and murder the builders.

nehemiah-4:5:1.summary: The day comes like a thief in the night; only the idea of an unexpected arrival is shared.

nehemiah-4:5:2.summary: Enemies “conceal themselves” and watch the psalmist, loosely like plotters planning to come unseen.

nehemiah-4:5:3.summary: Ahithophel plans to come upon David unexpectedly and strike; a similar surprise-attack strategy in another setting.

nehemiah-4:5:4.summary: Destruction comes and you “will certainly not know it,” a loose verbal echo of “they will neither know nor see.”

nehemiah-4:5:5.summary: A conspiracy to kill Paul; only a general theme of murderous plotting is shared.

nehemiah-4:5:6.summary: Israel’s ambush of Gibeah shares only the general idea of ambush, not the situation or parties.

nehemiah-4:6:0.summary: Laban changing Jacob’s wages; the “ten times” link is absent from the Saints source, which says “from every place.”
nehemiah-4:6:0.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.
nehemiah-4:6:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

nehemiah-4:6:1.summary: Job’s complaint against his friends; the “ten times” link is absent from the Saints source text.
nehemiah-4:6:1.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.
nehemiah-4:6:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

nehemiah-4:6:2.summary: Jacob’s wages changed; the source’s Saints wording has no “ten times” to connect them.
nehemiah-4:6:2.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.
nehemiah-4:6:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

nehemiah-4:6:3.summary: Israel tested God “this tenth time”; the source’s Saints wording has no matching number.
nehemiah-4:6:3.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.

nehemiah-4:7:1.summary: Taking up the full armor of God to stand against the devil, a spiritual application of arming defenders.

nehemiah-4:7:2.summary: Advice on mature thinking has no specific link to stationing armed people behind the wall.

nehemiah-4:7:3.summary: Jacob dividing his gift herds for Esau shares no specific element with arming defenders.

nehemiah-4:7:4.summary: Armed men each with “his sword” guard against night terror, a loose image of armed watchmen.

nehemiah-4:7:5.summary: A kind lender who manages words with judgment has no link to stationing armed defenders.

nehemiah-4:7:6.summary: Being prudent like snakes among wolves shares no specific element with arming the people.

nehemiah-4:7:7.summary: Hezekiah rebuilds Jerusalem’s wall and prepares weapons against an attacker, a close parallel to fortifying and arming Jerusalem.

nehemiah-4:8:0.summary: Joab urges courage to “show strength for our people and for the cities of our God,” like fighting for brothers and houses.
nehemiah-4:8:0.why: Similar battle exhortation for one’s people.

nehemiah-4:8:1.summary: “Do not fear them … the Lord is among us,” a close parallel to “Do not be afraid of them. Remember our God.”
nehemiah-4:8:1.why: Same exhortation to fear God, not enemies.

nehemiah-4:8:2.summary: God tells Israel “do not fear” because adversaries will perish; a general reassurance theme.

nehemiah-4:8:3.summary: “The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear,” a general expression of fearlessness through God.
nehemiah-4:8:3.why: General confidence in God against people.

nehemiah-4:8:4.summary: God’s works are “fearsome” and enemies submit, echoing “great and fearsome” only loosely.

nehemiah-4:8:5.summary: A prayer to God the Savior and hope of the earth lacks the “fearsome” wording in this reading.
nehemiah-4:8:5.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

nehemiah-4:8:6.summary: Do not fear those who kill the body but fear God; a general contrast of human and divine fear.

nehemiah-4:8:7.summary: Trust in the Lord’s name rather than chariots, a general theme of relying on God in battle.
nehemiah-4:8:7.why: Trust in God over military strength.

nehemiah-4:8:8.summary: “Fear not, neither be dismayed” before going up; a general reassurance formula.

nehemiah-4:8:9.summary: Hezekiah tells defenders of Jerusalem not to be terrified of the enemy, because more are with us, a close parallel exhortation.

nehemiah-4:8:10.summary: The Lord avenges on His adversaries with great strength, a general picture of God’s might over enemies.

nehemiah-4:8:11.summary: Calls God “the great and mighty and fearful God,” the formula behind “our God, great and fearsome.”

nehemiah-4:8:13.summary: Nehemiah’s own prayer calls God “the Great and Fearsome,” the same title he now urges the people to remember.
nehemiah-4:8:13.why: Same speaker using the same title.

nehemiah-4:8:14.summary: Moses’ terror at Sinai shares only the word field of fear, not the exhortation against enemies.

nehemiah-4:8:15.summary: The Almighty’s glory in the northern clouds has no specific link to the battle exhortation.

nehemiah-4:8:16.summary: “Whom will I fear?” expresses fearlessness through God, a general theme of the exhortation.

nehemiah-4:8:17.summary: Israel “forgot God” and feared the oppressor, the reverse of “Do not be afraid of them. Remember our God.”

nehemiah-4:8:18.summary: Serving God with reverence and awe; only the idea of a fearsome God is shared.

nehemiah-4:8:19.summary: “Do not be fainthearted or afraid, for the Lord your God is with you,” a general encouragement formula.

nehemiah-4:8:20.summary: “Neither cower nor fear them” because the Lord will fight with you, closely matching the call not to fear and to battle.

nehemiah-4:8:21.summary: The psalmist “remembered” God’s ancient works; only the act of remembering God is shared.

nehemiah-4:8:22.summary: Remembering the Lord’s works and asking “what god is great like our God,” loosely echoing “remember our God, great.”

nehemiah-4:8:23.summary: God’s works are “fearsome,” a loose echo of the source’s “great and fearsome” God.

nehemiah-4:8:24.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us,” a general assurance of God’s presence against enemies.

nehemiah-4:8:25.summary: Recalling the exodus under Moses shares only the idea of remembering, not the battle exhortation.

nehemiah-4:8:26.summary: A plea for God to rend heaven and shake nations has no specific link to Nehemiah’s exhortation.

nehemiah-4:8:27.summary: “Do not fear or be terrified before this great crowd,” for the battle belongs to God, a close parallel exhortation.
nehemiah-4:8:27.why: Parallel assurance before an enemy coalition.

nehemiah-4:8:28.summary: Judas tells his men they fight “for our lives and our customs,” like fighting for brothers, children, wives and houses.
nehemiah-4:8:28.why: Similar motive for a defensive fight.

nehemiah-4:9:0.summary: A call to fervent zeal has no specific link to returning to the wall after the plot failed.

nehemiah-4:9:1.summary: The Lord commanded that Ahithophel’s counsel “be scattered,” the same wording as God scattering the enemies’ counsel.

nehemiah-4:9:2.summary: “The Lord scatters the counsels of nations,” the same wording as God scattering their counsel.
nehemiah-4:9:2.why: States the principle seen in the event.

nehemiah-4:9:3.summary: God changes the counsels of the unscrupulous and confuses the devious, matching God thwarting the enemies’ plan.
nehemiah-4:9:3.why: God thwarts schemes of the wicked.

nehemiah-4:9:4.summary: God will “scatter” diviners’ signs and make counsel foolish; shared wording but a different target.

nehemiah-4:9:5.summary: David prays “scatter Ahithophel’s counsel,” the same idea of God scattering an enemy’s counsel.

nehemiah-4:9:6.summary: “Whatever counsel you devise, the Lord will scatter,” matching God scattering the enemies’ counsel.

nehemiah-4:9:7.summary: Nothing happens unless the Lord commands; only a general theme of divine sovereignty.

nehemiah-4:9:8.summary: There is no counsel with the impious; a loose link to the enemies’ failed counsel.

nehemiah-4:9:9.summary: Advice to work with one’s own hands has no real link to returning to the wall after danger.

nehemiah-4:9:10.summary: Slaves given “each his own work,” a verbal echo of “each to his work” in a different setting.
nehemiah-4:9:10.why: Image of each assigned his task.

nehemiah-4:9:11.summary: God catches the wise in their craftiness, a general theme of frustrated human schemes.

nehemiah-4:10:0.summary: Nehemiah and his guard stay armed and clothed, part of the same armed-work arrangement during the threat.

nehemiah-4:10:1.summary: Choosing faithful companions has no specific link to splitting workers between building and guarding.

nehemiah-4:10:2.summary: Mentions “shaken-out men” and the work on the wall, sharing terms but describing a different issue.

nehemiah-4:11:0.summary: “Share suffering as a good soldier,” a loose spiritual parallel to armed builders.

nehemiah-4:11:1.summary: Paul’s finished fight shares only a generic struggle metaphor with the armed builders.

nehemiah-4:11:2.summary: “Weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left,” loosely recalling work in one hand and a weapon in the other.
nehemiah-4:11:2.why: Image of weapons in both hands.

nehemiah-4:11:3.summary: Putting on the full armor of God, a spiritual application of builders who stay armed.

nehemiah-4:11:4.summary: “Stay awake; stand firm … be strong,” a general call to vigilant courage.

nehemiah-4:11:5.summary: An open door for work alongside “many opponents,” loosely like building amid enemies.

nehemiah-4:11:6.summary: Not frightened by opponents; a general theme of steadfastness under opposition.

nehemiah-4:11:7.summary: Paul forgoing his rights for the gospel has no specific link to armed builders.

nehemiah-4:11:8.summary: Promise that “you will build Jerusalem as a city,” a general link to rebuilding Jerusalem.

nehemiah-4:12:0.summary: Priests sound signal trumpets in battle and the Lord gives victory, loosely like the horn beside the builders.

nehemiah-4:12:1.summary: Signal trumpets in war bring deliverance from enemies, the law behind the horn-sounder and God fighting for His people.
nehemiah-4:12:1.why: Legal background for the trumpet signal.

nehemiah-4:14:0.summary: “The Lord shall fight for you,” the same assurance as “our God will wage war for us.”
nehemiah-4:14:0.why: Classic promise of God fighting for Israel.

nehemiah-4:14:2.summary: The Lord “shall Himself fight against them with you,” matching the assurance that God will wage war for us.

nehemiah-4:14:3.summary: “The Lord your God was fighting for you,” the same conviction behind Nehemiah’s assurance.
nehemiah-4:14:3.why: Recalls past experience of God fighting.

nehemiah-4:14:4.summary: “The Lord our God Himself shall fight for you,” closely matching “our God will wage war for us.”

nehemiah-4:14:5.summary: The Lord goes out and draws up for battle against the nations, an image of God fighting for Jerusalem.

nehemiah-4:14:6.summary: The Egyptians admit “the Lord is fighting for them,” the same reality Nehemiah promises.
nehemiah-4:14:6.why: Enemies recognize God fights for Israel.

nehemiah-4:15:0.summary: “Let us not grow weary in doing good,” a general parallel to tireless work from dawn to dusk.

nehemiah-4:15:1.summary: Paul labors and struggles by God’s power; only a general idea of strenuous labor.

nehemiah-4:15:2.summary: Be steadfast, abounding in the Lord’s work, a general parallel to persistent labor.

nehemiah-4:15:3.summary: Paul labored more than all by God’s grace; only a general idea of hard work.

nehemiah-4:16:0.summary: Later resettlement of people to live in Jerusalem; shares only the idea of people lodging in the city.

nehemiah-4:17:0.summary: Paul’s grace-driven labor has no specific link to Nehemiah’s guard never undressing.

nehemiah-4:17:1.summary: Abimelech leads by example, telling people to do as he did; a loose theme of leadership example.

nehemiah-4:17:2.summary: Song of righteous acts among Israel shares nothing specific with the guard’s vigilance.

nehemiah-4:17:3.summary: Nehemiah later appoints trusted men over Jerusalem; same leader and city but different situation.

nehemiah-4:17:4.summary: Nehemiah describes his own dedication to the wall work, matching his personal example here only generally.

nehemiah-5:1:0.summary: Israel produced “an outcry” instead of righteousness, the same kind of outcry from injustice within God’s people.

nehemiah-5:1:1.summary: Law requiring generosity to a needy brother, who may “cry against you unto the Lord,” the standard being breached.

nehemiah-5:1:2.summary: God brings justice for those who cry to Him; only a general theme of outcry.

nehemiah-5:1:3.summary: Moses asks, “you are brothers. Why are you wronging one another?” loosely matching conflict among brothers.

nehemiah-5:1:4.summary: Cries of defrauded laborers reach the Lord, a general theme of economic oppression’s outcry.

nehemiah-5:1:5.summary: Brothers defraud brothers, a general parallel to the people’s complaint against their Jewish brothers.

nehemiah-5:1:6.summary: Job’s oath about land groaning and landowners has no specific link to the outcry against brothers.

nehemiah-5:1:7.summary: Law against pressing a poor brother with interest, who “cries to Me,” the very abuse behind this outcry.

nehemiah-5:1:8.summary: Forbids taking interest from a poor brother, the law at stake in the outcry against fellow Jews.

nehemiah-5:1:9.summary: God hears the cry of the poor; only a general theme of outcry.

nehemiah-5:1:10.summary: God heard His people’s cry under Egyptian taskmasters; a general theme of outcry from oppression.

nehemiah-5:2:0.summary: Blessing of eating one’s labor and many sons has no real link to the famine complaint.

nehemiah-5:2:1.summary: Curse on priests’ blessings shares nothing specific with families needing grain.

nehemiah-5:2:2.summary: Jacob sends for grain “that we may live and not die,” loosely echoing “obtain grain, eat, and live.”

nehemiah-5:2:3.summary: Sons as the Lord’s reward has no real link to large families needing grain.

nehemiah-5:2:4.summary: Judah urges going for food “that we may live and not die,” a loose famine parallel.

nehemiah-5:2:5.summary: All countries come to buy grain in famine; only a general famine theme.

nehemiah-5:3:0.summary: Laws for a brother who becomes poor and is sold, the protections relevant to families pledging property for grain.

nehemiah-5:3:1.summary: Defrauding God of tithes has no specific link to pledging fields for grain.

nehemiah-5:3:2.summary: Do not close your hand to a needy brother, a general principle for those forced to pledge property.

nehemiah-5:3:3.summary: Famine forces Egyptians to give livestock for bread, a similar slide into surrendering property for food (shown portion only).

nehemiah-5:4:0.summary: Mentions taxes owed to the king, sharing the royal-tax theme but in an accusation letter.

nehemiah-5:4:1.summary: Refers to taxes paid to kings, a general link to the king’s taxes burdening the people.

nehemiah-5:4:2.summary: Serving enemies in want as a covenant curse, a general theme of foreign burdens.

nehemiah-5:4:3.summary: Kings set over Judah “exercise authority over our bodies and our livestock,” the same imperial burden behind borrowing for taxes.

nehemiah-5:4:4.summary: Canaanites remaining in Gezer shares nothing specific with borrowing for the king’s taxes.

nehemiah-5:4:5.summary: Exempts temple staff from tax, sharing only the Persian tax theme.

nehemiah-5:4:6.summary: Solomon’s forced tribute on remaining peoples has no specific link to Judean debt for royal taxes.

nehemiah-5:5:1.summary: A lender comes to take a widow’s two sons as slaves, the same debt slavery of children described here.

nehemiah-5:5:2.summary: Do not overlook “those belonging to your own family”; a general call to care for kin.

nehemiah-5:5:3.summary: Brothers sell Joseph, “our brother and our flesh,” matching the complaint of selling one’s own flesh into slavery.
nehemiah-5:5:3.why: Classic case of selling a brother.

nehemiah-5:5:4.summary: “You are of my bones and of my flesh” shares only the kinship-flesh idiom.

nehemiah-5:5:5.summary: A debtor is ordered sold with wife and children, the same debt-slavery of families.

nehemiah-5:5:6.summary: Laws on Hebrew slaves and on selling a daughter, governing the very servitude described (shown portion).

nehemiah-5:5:7.summary: The rich oppress the poor, a general theme matching the honored men’s control of fields.

nehemiah-5:6:0.summary: Moses leaves Pharaoh in anger; the Saints source speaks of grief, so only a strong reaction is shared.

nehemiah-5:6:1.summary: Nehemiah later contends fiercely with offenders, a similar reaction by the same leader to a different wrong.

nehemiah-5:6:2.summary: Moses was “deeply distressed” at rebels, a loose echo of “deeply grieved.”

nehemiah-5:6:3.summary: “Be angry and do not sin”; the Saints source speaks of grief, so only righteous emotion is shared.

nehemiah-5:6:4.summary: Nehemiah finds Tobia’s use of the chamber “exceedingly evil,” a similar reaction by him to a different wrong.

nehemiah-5:6:5.summary: Jesus is grieved at hardness of hearts, a loose parallel to grief at the people’s outcry.

nehemiah-5:7:0.summary: “You shall not charge your brother interest,” the law behind Nehemiah’s charge of demands against brothers.

nehemiah-5:7:1.summary: Take no interest from your brother and fear God, the law behind the rebuke of demands against brothers.

nehemiah-5:7:3.summary: Taking interest and oppressing as Jerusalem’s sin, a general parallel to the nobles’ demands.

nehemiah-5:7:4.summary: Judge justly without favouring the mighty; only a general justice theme.

nehemiah-5:7:5.summary: Jehoshaphat charges judges to act justly; only a general justice theme.

nehemiah-5:7:6.summary: The righteous do not lend silver at interest, a general principle relevant to the nobles’ demands.

nehemiah-5:7:7.summary: Rules limiting how pledges are taken from a debtor, generally related to the pledged property.

nehemiah-5:7:8.summary: “You shall not exact it of your brother,” closely matching the charge of demands “each against his brother.”
nehemiah-5:7:8.why: Law on releasing a brother’s debt.

nehemiah-5:7:9.summary: God rebukes judges and calls them to rescue the needy, a general parallel to rebuking leaders.

nehemiah-5:7:10.summary: Paul opposes Cephas to his face, a general parallel to confronting leaders.

nehemiah-5:7:11.summary: Reprove sinners “before all,” loosely matching the great assembly convened against the nobles.

nehemiah-5:7:12.summary: Knowing no one according to the flesh shares nothing specific with the rebuke of nobles.

nehemiah-5:7:13.summary: Who may dwell on God’s holy mountain has no specific link to Nehemiah’s rebuke.

nehemiah-5:7:14.summary: Oded rebukes Israel for making brethren male and female slaves, a close parallel to Nehemiah’s rebuke.

nehemiah-5:7:15.summary: Rulers told to remove oppression from God’s people, a general parallel to rebuking leaders.
nehemiah-5:7:15.why: Call to rulers to stop oppression.

nehemiah-5:7:16.summary: Open rebukes are better; only a general theme of rebuke.

nehemiah-5:7:17.summary: Bringing an offender before the Church, loosely like convening an assembly.

nehemiah-5:7:18.summary: “My heart said” shares only a heart idiom with “my heart took counsel.”

nehemiah-5:7:19.summary: Rebuke with all authority; only a general theme of rebuke.

nehemiah-5:7:20.summary: “Be angry, and do not sin; speak in your hearts” shares only incidental heart wording.

nehemiah-5:8:1.summary: Giving according to readiness has no specific link to redeeming sold Jews.

nehemiah-5:8:2.summary: Death penalty for one who subjugates and “sells” a brother Israelite, the offense Nehemiah condemns.

nehemiah-5:8:3.summary: Grieving a brother over food shares only the word “brother.”

nehemiah-5:8:4.summary: Destroying the weak brother through knowledge shares only the word “brother.”

nehemiah-5:8:5.summary: Listeners’ tongues clung to their throats, loosely like the nobles falling quiet.

nehemiah-5:8:6.summary: The guest without a wedding garment was speechless, loosely like finding no answer.

nehemiah-5:8:7.summary: Taking from the one who has not shares nothing specific with selling brothers.

nehemiah-5:8:8.summary: Job’s friends “answered no more,” loosely like the nobles who fell quiet and found no answer.

nehemiah-5:8:9.summary: The parable’s distribution of talents shares nothing specific with buying back sold Jews.

nehemiah-5:8:10.summary: The law stops “every mouth,” loosely matching the nobles left with no answer.

nehemiah-5:8:11.summary: Death for one who steals “one of the sons of Israel” and sells him, the law condemning selling brothers.

nehemiah-5:8:12.summary: Doing good especially to the household of faith shares only a general kinship idea.

nehemiah-5:9:1.summary: David’s deed “provoked the Lord’s enemies,” loosely like wrongdoing that brings reproach from enemies.

nehemiah-5:9:2.summary: God’s name is blasphemed “among the nations because of you,” matching the call to avoid the nations’ reproach.
nehemiah-5:9:2.why: Conduct affects God’s reputation among nations.

nehemiah-5:9:3.summary: Shares only the phrase “not good” in a saying about partial judgment.

nehemiah-5:9:4.summary: Keep good conduct among the Gentiles who slander you, the same concern for outsiders’ reproach.

nehemiah-5:9:5.summary: Conduct so that God’s word “may not be reviled,” a general concern about outsiders’ reproach.

nehemiah-5:9:7.summary: The Church walks “in the fear of the Lord,” sharing only the fear-of-God phrase.
nehemiah-5:9:7.why: Fear of God as a way of life.

nehemiah-5:9:8.summary: Eli tells his exploiting sons the report is “not good. Do not act this way,” closely echoing “not good. Not so!”

nehemiah-5:9:9.summary: Abraham assumes “no reverence for God” in Gerar; only the fear-of-God idea is shared.
nehemiah-5:9:9.why: Fear of God as moral restraint.

nehemiah-5:9:10.summary: Strife among brothers while Canaanites lived in the land, loosely like internal wrongs before watching nations.
nehemiah-5:9:10.why: Brothers should not quarrel before outsiders.

nehemiah-5:9:12.summary: Joseph says “I fear God” as a basis for fair dealing; only the fear-of-God motive is shared.

nehemiah-5:9:13.summary: Shares only the phrase “not good” in a saying about penalizing the righteous.

nehemiah-5:9:14.summary: Nehemiah refrained from exactions “because of the fear of God,” the same motive he urges on the nobles.

nehemiah-5:9:15.summary: A lawless man leading friends astray shares only the words “not good.”

nehemiah-5:9:16.summary: Nehemiah prays against the enemies’ “reproach” and mockery, the same reproach of enemies he now warns about.

nehemiah-5:9:17.summary: Give “the opponent no opportunity for abuse,” a general concern about outsiders’ criticism.

nehemiah-5:9:18.summary: Israel profaned God’s name among the nations, a general parallel to bringing reproach before them.

nehemiah-5:10:0.summary: Urging not to receive grace in vain shares nothing specific with relinquishing exactions.

nehemiah-5:10:2.summary: Paul persuades people knowing the fear of the Lord; only general persuasion is shared.
nehemiah-5:10:2.why: Persuasion grounded in fear of God.

nehemiah-5:10:3.summary: Paul appeals rather than commands, loosely like Nehemiah’s “Let us, I pray” appeal.

nehemiah-5:10:4.summary: Paul did not use his right to support, loosely like leaders relinquishing their claims (shown portion).

nehemiah-5:10:5.summary: Nehemiah’s charge of “making demands” against brothers, the same exaction he now asks them to relinquish.

nehemiah-5:10:6.summary: One who “gave at interest and took increase” will not live, a general condemnation of the exaction.

nehemiah-5:10:7.summary: The righteous will not give silver at interest, a general principle behind relinquishing the exaction.

nehemiah-5:10:8.summary: Paul begging people to be reconciled to God shares only the act of appealing.

nehemiah-5:10:9.summary: The righteous does not lend silver at interest, a general principle relevant to the exaction.

nehemiah-5:10:10.summary: “Collect nothing beyond what has been appointed … Extort from no one,” a general call against exaction.

nehemiah-5:10:11.summary: People planning evil on their beds shares nothing specific with relinquishing the exaction in the shown text.

nehemiah-5:11:0.summary: Undo “coercive agreements” and tear up “every unjust written contract,” matching the restoration of pledged property.
nehemiah-5:11:0.why: Prophetic call to cancel oppressive debts.

nehemiah-5:11:1.summary: Law requiring return of what was obtained by wrong, loosely like restoring fields and houses.

nehemiah-5:11:2.summary: Samuel offers to “repay” anyone he squeezed; only a general restitution theme.

nehemiah-5:11:3.summary: Repaying the ewe lamb sevenfold shares only a general idea of repayment.

nehemiah-5:11:5.summary: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance,” a general link to restoring what was taken.

nehemiah-5:12:0.summary: Esdras made the leaders and priests “swear to act according to this word,” the same oath formula.

nehemiah-5:12:1.summary: Judah’s magnates covenanted to free Hebrew slaves but “turned back,” the broken pledge Nehemiah guards against by an oath.

nehemiah-5:12:2.summary: The assembly agrees to carry out “this word,” a parallel collective assent to a reform.

nehemiah-5:12:3.summary: The high priest adjuring Jesus shares only the idea of an oath.

nehemiah-5:12:4.summary: The rich young man would not give up property, the opposite of nobles agreeing to return it.

nehemiah-5:12:5.summary: Josiah leads the people into a covenant before the Lord, a general parallel to a sworn commitment.

nehemiah-5:12:6.summary: The people “swore by the Lord” to seek Him, a general parallel to a sworn pledge.

nehemiah-5:12:7.summary: The people enter a curse and oath to keep God’s law, a later general sworn covenant.

nehemiah-5:12:8.summary: An oath sworn before the altar, with God judging, a general background for binding oaths.

nehemiah-5:12:9.summary: Nehemiah again “made them swear by God” to end a wrong, the same leader using an oath to enforce reform.

nehemiah-5:12:10.summary: Zacchaeus vows to repay anything he extorted, a parallel voluntary restitution of exacted goods.

nehemiah-5:12:11.summary: Captive brethren are released and provided for, a general parallel to freeing oppressed brothers.

nehemiah-5:12:12.summary: The covenant pledges to “release the seventh year and the demand of every hand,” formalizing the debt relief agreed here.
nehemiah-5:12:12.why: Later formal commitment to debt release.

nehemiah-5:13:0.summary: Paul “shook out his garments” as a sign against opponents, the same symbolic act as shaking out the wrap.

nehemiah-5:13:1.summary: Shaking dust off the feet as a sign against rejecters, a related but different gesture.

nehemiah-5:13:2.summary: A curse enters the house of the false swearer and destroys it, like God shaking out the house of the oath-breaker.

nehemiah-5:13:3.summary: “All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’ And they praised the Lord,” the same response as the assembly’s.
nehemiah-5:13:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

nehemiah-5:13:4.summary: The woman responds “So be it” to a curse, a loose parallel to the assembly’s Amen to the curse.

nehemiah-5:13:5.summary: All the people answered “Amen” and worshiped, the same communal response later in Nehemiah.

nehemiah-5:13:6.summary: Pay your vows to the Most High; a general theme of keeping vows.

nehemiah-5:13:7.summary: Better not to vow than to vow and not pay, a general warning matching the oath’s seriousness.

nehemiah-5:13:8.summary: Ahijah tears his garment as a sign, a general parallel to a symbolic garment act.

nehemiah-5:13:10.summary: The people “stood in the covenant,” a general parallel to the people carrying out the word.

nehemiah-5:13:11.summary: Shaking dust from the feet against opponents, a related but different symbolic gesture.

nehemiah-5:13:12.summary: “I have sworn and established it” to keep God’s judgments; only a general oath theme.

nehemiah-5:13:13.summary: The kingdom torn from Saul; the shown text lacks any garment gesture or oath link.

nehemiah-5:13:14.summary: Make vows and repay the Lord; only a general vow theme.

nehemiah-5:14:1.summary: Paul has a right to eat and drink but did not use it, matching Nehemiah not eating the governor’s provision (shown portion).

nehemiah-5:14:2.summary: Paul did not “eat anyone’s bread without payment” so as not to burden, like Nehemiah declining the provision.

nehemiah-5:14:3.summary: Paul offers the gospel without charge, not using his right, a general parallel.

nehemiah-5:14:4.summary: Dates Nehemiah’s commission to “the twentieth year of King Arthasastha,” the start of the twelve years mentioned.

nehemiah-5:14:5.summary: Paying taxes to authorities shares only a general tax idea, not the refusal of provision.

nehemiah-5:14:6.summary: Accusation about lost royal taxes has no specific link to Nehemiah declining his provision.

nehemiah-5:15:0.summary: Nehemiah urges the nobles to act “in the fear of our God,” the motive he says governed his own conduct.

nehemiah-5:15:2.summary: “Who among you fears the Lord?” shares only the fear-of-God theme.

nehemiah-5:15:3.summary: Job says “fear of the Lord gripped me,” restraining him from wrongdoing, loosely like Nehemiah’s restraint.

nehemiah-5:15:4.summary: “Fear God and keep His commandments”; only a general fear-of-God theme.

nehemiah-5:15:5.summary: Doing more than others do; a loose link to Nehemiah not acting like former governors.

nehemiah-5:15:6.summary: Paul “burdened no one” and kept himself from being a burden, matching Nehemiah not laying burdens on the people.

nehemiah-5:15:7.summary: The Lord delights in those who fear Him; only a general fear-of-God theme.

nehemiah-5:15:8.summary: Paul “did not burden you,” the same refusal to burden those he led.

nehemiah-5:15:9.summary: Under an unjust ruler all subordinates are lawless, loosely like former governors’ men abusing authority.

nehemiah-5:15:10.summary: A king will take produce for his servants, a general picture of rulers’ exactions.

nehemiah-5:15:11.summary: Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; only a general fear-of-God theme.

nehemiah-5:15:12.summary: Priests’ servants take by force, loosely like governors’ men exercising authority over people.

nehemiah-5:15:13.summary: A judge who “neither feared God” nor respected people, the opposite of Nehemiah’s God-fearing restraint.

nehemiah-5:16:0.summary: Not growing weary in doing good shares nothing specific with Nehemiah acquiring no field.

nehemiah-5:16:1.summary: All seek their own interests, the opposite of Nehemiah’s refusal to profit.

nehemiah-5:16:2.summary: Paul came with no “pretext for greed,” a general parallel to Nehemiah acquiring no field.

nehemiah-5:16:3.summary: General call to abound in the Lord’s work shares only the word “work.”

nehemiah-5:16:4.summary: Paul “coveted no one’s silver” and worked to support others, matching Nehemiah taking nothing for himself.

nehemiah-5:16:5.summary: Perseverance in good work for eternal life shares only the word “work.”

nehemiah-5:16:6.summary: Moses says “I have taken no desirable possession from any of them,” matching Nehemiah acquiring no field.

nehemiah-5:16:7.summary: The parable’s good soil shares nothing specific with Nehemiah’s conduct.

nehemiah-5:16:8.summary: Paul did not take advantage of people through his associates, loosely like Nehemiah’s men serving the work.

nehemiah-5:17:0.summary: Prophets who eat at Jezebel’s table; only a large royal table is shared.

nehemiah-5:17:1.summary: David invites Mephibosheth to eat “at my table continually,” a general parallel of a ruler’s hospitality.

nehemiah-5:17:2.summary: “Be hospitable to one another,” a general link to Nehemiah’s table.

nehemiah-5:17:3.summary: “Pursue hospitality,” a general link to Nehemiah feeding many.

nehemiah-5:17:4.summary: The devout making wise plans has no link to Nehemiah’s table in this reading.
nehemiah-5:17:4.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

nehemiah-5:17:5.summary: Mephibosheth “ate continually at the king’s table,” a general parallel of a ruler’s table.

nehemiah-5:18:0.summary: Solomon’s daily provisions of cattle and sheep, a parallel record of a ruler’s daily table requirements.

nehemiah-5:18:1.summary: The righteous has compassion and gives; only a general generosity theme.

nehemiah-5:18:2.summary: The righteous shows mercy and lends; only a general generosity theme.

nehemiah-5:19:0.summary: “Remember me, our God, for goodness,” Nehemiah’s same closing prayer.

nehemiah-5:19:1.summary: “Remember us, Lord,” a general echo of asking God to remember.

nehemiah-5:19:3.summary: “In these things remember me, O God,” Nehemiah’s same prayer after a reform.

nehemiah-5:19:4.summary: God’s plan of peace for exiles shares nothing specific with Nehemiah’s prayer to be remembered.

nehemiah-5:19:5.summary: “Remember me Thyself, for Thy kindness’ sake,” a general echo of asking God to remember.

nehemiah-5:19:6.summary: A plea of the poor for help lacks the remembrance wording in this reading.
nehemiah-5:19:6.why: Link depends on wording absent here.

nehemiah-5:19:7.summary: The Lord repays according to righteousness, a general basis for asking reward for good deeds.

nehemiah-5:19:8.summary: Even a cup of water “will certainly not lose his reward,” a general theme of God rewarding good.

nehemiah-5:19:9.summary: Giving a cup of cold water will not lose its reward, a general theme of God rewarding good.

nehemiah-5:19:10.summary: The King rewards those who fed and clothed others, a general theme of reward for service.

nehemiah-5:19:11.summary: Joseph asks the cupbearer “remember me,” a verbal echo in a human rather than divine plea.

nehemiah-5:9:11.summary: Proverbs 19:2 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
nehemiah-5:9:11.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
nehemiah-5:9:11.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

nehemiah-5:15:1.summary: Proverbs 16:6 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
nehemiah-5:15:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
nehemiah-5:15:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

nehemiah-6:1:0.summary: Sanaballat, Tobia and “Gesam the Arabi heard,” the same three opponents reacting to the work.

nehemiah-6:1:1.summary: Sanaballat and Tobia first “heard” and were displeased, the start of the same opposition.

nehemiah-6:1:2.summary: Sanaballat “heard that we were building the wall” and was angry, an earlier stage of the same reaction.

nehemiah-6:1:3.summary: The Fish Gate’s builders “set up its doors,” the gate doors still not set at this point.

nehemiah-6:1:4.summary: Sanaballat, Tobia and the Arabs “heard” of the walls’ progress, an earlier stage of the same reaction.

nehemiah-6:1:5.summary: The priests built the Sheep Gate and “set up its doors,” the gate-door work referred to here.

nehemiah-6:1:6.summary: The gate of Isana was repaired and its doors set up, the gate-door work referred to here.

nehemiah-6:1:7.summary: Promise to “build Jerusalem as a city,” a general link to the completed wall.

nehemiah-6:2:0.summary: Records who built “Ono,” the same place where the enemies proposed to meet.

nehemiah-6:2:1.summary: The sinner watches the righteous closely, a general theme of enemies plotting harm.

nehemiah-6:2:3.summary: Deceitful lips speaking “with a heart and a heart,” a general theme of duplicitous invitation.

nehemiah-6:2:4.summary: An enemy entreats with his lips while devising deceits, “do not be persuaded,” fitting the false invitation to Ono.

nehemiah-6:2:5.summary: Joab greets Amasa warmly before killing him, a general parallel to a friendly pretext hiding harm.

nehemiah-6:2:6.summary: Spies pretending to be righteous to trap Jesus, a general parallel to a feigned approach.

nehemiah-6:2:7.summary: Toil as rivalry with a companion shares nothing specific with the plot at Ono.

nehemiah-6:2:8.summary: Hearers who will not obey shares nothing specific with the enemies’ invitation.

nehemiah-6:2:9.summary: “Do not put confidence in friends,” a general warning about trusting others.

nehemiah-6:2:10.summary: The sinner observes the righteous and seeks his death, a general parallel to planning harm.

nehemiah-6:2:11.summary: Ishmael’s men kill Gedaliah, the appointed governor of the land, a loose parallel to a plot against Judah’s governor.

nehemiah-6:2:12.summary: Joab takes Abner aside “to speak with him while lying in wait,” a general parallel to a meeting masking harm.

nehemiah-6:3:0.summary: Be prudent as snakes among wolves, a general parallel to Nehemiah’s wary refusal.

nehemiah-6:3:1.summary: We must work while it is day, a general theme of urgency in God’s work.

nehemiah-6:3:2.summary: Be absorbed in your work; only a general theme of devotion to a task.

nehemiah-6:3:3.summary: The man who “began to build and was unable to finish,” a contrast to Nehemiah’s resolve to finish.

nehemiah-6:3:4.summary: Do whatever your hand finds with your strength, a general theme of wholehearted work.

nehemiah-6:3:5.summary: The resourceful reconsider rather than believe every word; a general theme of discernment.

nehemiah-6:4:0.summary: The widow’s repeated coming wears down the judge; only a general theme of persistent requests.

nehemiah-6:4:1.summary: A seductress leading a youth astray shares nothing specific with the repeated messages.

nehemiah-6:4:2.summary: Delilah’s repeated attempts to trap Samson, a general parallel to repeated enticing messages.

nehemiah-6:4:3.summary: “We did not yield to them,” a general parallel to Nehemiah’s steady refusals.

nehemiah-6:4:4.summary: Be “steadfast, immovable,” a general theme matching Nehemiah’s unchanged answer.

nehemiah-6:4:5.summary: The resourceful reconsider rather than believe every word; a general theme of discernment.

nehemiah-6:4:6.summary: Delilah’s request to learn how to bind Samson, a general parallel to an enticement hiding harm.

nehemiah-6:4:7.summary: Samson gives way under repeated pressure, the opposite of Nehemiah’s unchanged answer (shown portion).

nehemiah-6:5:0.summary: Deception of the perishing shares nothing specific with Sanaballat sending an open letter.

nehemiah-6:5:1.summary: False apostles disguised as righteous shares nothing specific with the open letter in the shown verse.

nehemiah-6:5:2.summary: An enemy’s envoy speaks publicly to those on the wall, loosely like an open message meant for public hearing.

nehemiah-6:5:3.summary: Not unaware of Satan’s designs; a general theme of recognizing schemes.

nehemiah-6:5:4.summary: Stand against the devil’s schemes; a general theme of resisting schemes.

nehemiah-6:6:0.summary: The same enemies voice the same charge of revolt, asking “Are you revolting against the king?”
nehemiah-6:6:0.why: Shows the revolt accusation was a recurring tactic.

nehemiah-6:6:1.summary: Both concern being slandered with false claims, but the settings and charges differ.
nehemiah-6:6:1.why: General parallel of slander against the faithful.

nehemiah-6:6:2.summary: Shares the general idea of being “slandered” falsely, without the political charge of revolt.
nehemiah-6:6:2.why: Offers a response to false accusation.

nehemiah-6:6:4.summary: Speaks of people who “falsely speak every evil thing,” a general parallel to the invented report.

nehemiah-6:6:5.summary: General lament over deceitful tongues among neighbors; no link to the revolt report or wall-building.
nehemiah-6:6:5.why: Only a broad theme of falsehood.

nehemiah-6:6:6.summary: Mentions slander as evildoers and submission to a king, loosely echoing the charge of rebellion.
nehemiah-6:6:6.why: Loose parallel on slander and loyalty to rulers.

nehemiah-6:6:7.summary: Same episode: Sanaballat, Tobia and Gesam hear of the wall and plot harm against Nehemiah.
nehemiah-6:6:7.why: Gives the immediate context of the letter.

nehemiah-6:6:8.summary: Pilate sitting at the judgment seat shares nothing with the shown verse beyond a trial setting.
nehemiah-6:6:8.why: The shown text lacks the kingship charge.

nehemiah-6:6:9.summary: Earlier enemies also accuse Jerusalem's builders of being “rebellious” and harmful to kings.
nehemiah-6:6:9.why: Shows a pattern of rebellion charges against rebuilding.

nehemiah-6:6:10.summary: Jesus is falsely accused of political subversion and of claiming to be “a king,” like Nehemiah.
nehemiah-6:6:10.why: Parallel false charge of royal pretension.

nehemiah-6:6:11.summary: “Bad report” and being called deceivers loosely parallel the false report about Nehemiah.
nehemiah-6:6:11.why: General theme of enduring evil report.

nehemiah-6:6:12.summary: Enemies gather and plot against Jeremiah, a general parallel to schemes against Nehemiah.
nehemiah-6:6:12.why: Broad theme of plotting against God's servant.

nehemiah-6:7:0.summary: A deceitful enemy who speaks fair words while devising deceit loosely fits the invitation to “take counsel.”

nehemiah-6:7:1.summary: Absalom's agents proclaim him king, a loose parallel to the alleged plan to be proclaimed king.
nehemiah-6:7:1.why: Example of a real royal conspiracy.

nehemiah-6:7:2.summary: Adonijah becomes king without the king knowing, loosely parallel to an alleged rival kingship.
nehemiah-6:7:2.why: General theme of usurpation reported to a king.

nehemiah-6:7:3.summary: Conspirators propose a pretext meeting to kill Paul, loosely like the invitation to “take counsel.”

nehemiah-6:7:4.summary: Adonijah's supporters acclaim “Long live King Adonijah,” loosely echoing the alleged proclamation.

nehemiah-6:7:5.summary: A prophet anoints and proclaims a king, loosely matching the charge that prophets would proclaim Nehemiah.
nehemiah-6:7:5.why: Shows prophets' role in proclaiming kings.

nehemiah-6:7:7.summary: Adonijah conferring with supporters is only a distant parallel to alleged royal plotting.

nehemiah-6:8:0.summary: A tongue that “devised injustice” loosely parallels words “falsely devising” from the heart.

nehemiah-6:8:1.summary: The Greek reading “unjust physicians” does not carry the Hebrew “forgers of lies” link to false invention.
nehemiah-6:8:1.why: Link depends on wording absent here.
nehemiah-6:8:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

nehemiah-6:8:2.summary: People who “speak emptiness” and conceive trouble loosely parallel invented accusations.
nehemiah-6:8:2.why: General theme of empty, false speech.

nehemiah-6:8:3.summary: Paul denies charges his accusers cannot prove, similar to Nehemiah denying the fabricated report.

nehemiah-6:8:4.summary: Speech coming from the heart loosely echoes words devised “from your own heart.”
nehemiah-6:8:4.why: General point on speech revealing the heart.

nehemiah-6:8:5.summary: Enemies who “spoke vain things and meditated on deceptions” broadly parallel the fabricated report.

nehemiah-6:8:6.summary: Paul asserts his innocence of wrongdoing against the Jews, loosely like Nehemiah's denial.

nehemiah-6:8:7.summary: Kings speaking falsely at one table is unrelated beyond the word “falsely.”

nehemiah-6:8:8.summary: Words of “lawlessness and deceit” broadly parallel the enemies' false claims.

nehemiah-6:8:9.summary: Accusations “they could not prove” parallel the unfounded report against Nehemiah.

nehemiah-6:8:10.summary: The liar speaks “from what is his own,” loosely echoing lies devised from one's own heart.
nehemiah-6:8:10.why: Traces lies to their inner source.

nehemiah-6:9:0.summary: God gives “strength in my soul,” a general parallel to Nehemiah's strengthening.

nehemiah-6:9:1.summary: Power made complete in weakness is a broad theme related to strengthening under pressure.

nehemiah-6:9:2.summary: David, threatened by his people, “was strengthened in the Lord,” paralleling strengthening amid intimidation.
nehemiah-6:9:2.why: Model of a leader strengthened under threat.

nehemiah-6:9:3.summary: A general call to “be strengthened,” without the specific setting of intimidation.

nehemiah-6:9:4.summary: God will “strengthen” sufferers, a general parallel.

nehemiah-6:9:5.summary: Strength for all things through God is only a general parallel.

nehemiah-6:9:6.summary: Same wall project: enemies plan to “bring the work to a stop” and Judah fears they cannot build.
nehemiah-6:9:6.why: Earlier phase of the same intimidation campaign.

nehemiah-6:9:7.summary: “Do not fear... I strengthened you” broadly parallels resisting fear with strength.
nehemiah-6:9:7.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

nehemiah-6:9:8.summary: Prayer to be “strengthened with power” is a general parallel.

nehemiah-6:9:9.summary: Both use the image of drooping or slack “hands” that must be strengthened.

nehemiah-6:9:10.summary: “Be strong, limp hands... do not fear!” matches slack hands and the response to fear.
nehemiah-6:9:10.why: Same image of weak hands and fear.

nehemiah-6:9:11.summary: “Do not let your hands grow feeble... your work” matches hands growing slack from the work.
nehemiah-6:9:11.why: Close verbal echo about hands and work.

nehemiah-6:9:12.summary: Opponents claim Jeremiah “weakens the hands” of the people, the same intimidation idiom.

nehemiah-6:9:13.summary: A plea of hope not to be disgraced has no specific link to strengthening hands against intimidation.

nehemiah-6:9:14.summary: Same episode: the prophets who were “frightening me,” naming the same intimidation.

nehemiah-6:9:16.summary: Fear met by hope in God loosely parallels responding to intimidation.
nehemiah-6:9:16.why: General theme of trust amid fear.

nehemiah-6:9:17.summary: God gives “power and strengthening” to His people, a general parallel.

nehemiah-6:9:18.summary: Enemies shout to people on the wall “to frighten” them, the same tactic against Jerusalem.

nehemiah-6:9:19.summary: God promises to “strengthen them,” a general parallel.

nehemiah-6:10:0.summary: Jeremiah is “under guard and cannot enter the Lord's house,” loosely echoing Semei being “confined.”

nehemiah-6:10:1.summary: Warning about false prophets loosely fits Semei, later exposed as hired, but is not specific.

nehemiah-6:10:2.summary: The sinner watching the righteous closely is a general parallel to plots against Nehemiah.

nehemiah-6:10:3.summary: Deceitful lips speaking empty things broadly fit Semei's false warning.

nehemiah-6:10:4.summary: Shares only the incidental word “confined” in an unrelated judgment on Ahab's house.

nehemiah-6:10:5.summary: A prophet told to “be shut inside your house” loosely parallels Semei being confined.
nehemiah-6:10:5.why: Possible parallel of a prophet shut in.

nehemiah-6:10:6.summary: Hezekiah opening the temple doors is unrelated beyond the doors of the Lord's house.

nehemiah-6:10:7.summary: A different man named Samaia in Ezra's list; no connection to Semei son of Dalaia.

nehemiah-6:10:8.summary: Temple doors shut during a plot against Paul; only a loose setting parallel.

nehemiah-6:10:9.summary: Shut doors as a cultic rebuke is unrelated to hiding in the temple.

nehemiah-6:10:10.summary: The impious mouth as “a trap” loosely fits Semei's deceptive advice.

nehemiah-6:10:11.summary: Joash hidden in the Lord's house from murder is a loose parallel to hiding in the temple.
nehemiah-6:10:11.why: Contrasting legitimate refuge in the temple.

nehemiah-6:10:12.summary: Ahaz shutting the temple doors is unrelated beyond the shared phrase.

nehemiah-6:10:13.summary: Temple side chambers have no real link to the proposed hiding place.

nehemiah-6:10:14.summary: Hating the light is unrelated to the night plot or the temple scheme.

nehemiah-6:10:15.summary: Prayer against “a deceitful tongue” broadly fits the deceitful counsel.

nehemiah-6:10:17.summary: Evildoers working at night in darkness loosely parallels coming “at night to murder.”
nehemiah-6:10:17.why: Only the night-time menace is shared.

nehemiah-6:10:18.summary: Another Samaia in a list of names; no connection to this episode.

nehemiah-6:10:19.summary: Shut sanctuary doors in Ahaz's apostasy are unrelated beyond wording.

nehemiah-6:11:0.summary: The righteous person “confident like a lion” loosely parallels Nehemiah's refusal to hide in fear.
nehemiah-6:11:0.why: Frames Nehemiah's courage as righteous confidence.

nehemiah-6:11:1.summary: The psalmist refuses advice to flee from those plotting in the dark, loosely like Nehemiah's refusal.
nehemiah-6:11:1.why: Parallel refusal to flee from threat.

nehemiah-6:11:2.summary: Paul's readiness to die in Jerusalem loosely parallels Nehemiah's refusal to save his life improperly.
nehemiah-6:11:2.why: General theme of courage despite danger.

nehemiah-6:11:3.summary: Being poured out as an offering has no specific link to refusing to enter the house.

nehemiah-6:11:4.summary: The righteous person “will never be shaken,” a general parallel to Nehemiah's steadiness.

nehemiah-6:11:5.summary: Paul values completing his ministry over his life, loosely like Nehemiah putting the work first.
nehemiah-6:11:5.why: General theme of courage for one's task.

nehemiah-6:11:6.summary: The established heart that “shall certainly not fear” broadly fits Nehemiah's resolve.

nehemiah-6:11:7.summary: Jesus, warned that Herod wants to kill Him, refuses to leave; a loose parallel to rejecting a fearful warning.
nehemiah-6:11:7.why: Parallel response to a warning of murder.

nehemiah-6:11:8.summary: Moses “not fearing the king's anger” is a general parallel of courage.

nehemiah-6:11:9.summary: Risking life “for the work” loosely echoes Nehemiah's devotion to the work.
nehemiah-6:11:9.why: General theme of risk for God's work.

nehemiah-6:11:10.summary: A proverb about flies spoiling oil has no link to this verse.

nehemiah-6:11:11.summary: Eliphaz's rebuke about Job's fear has no specific link to Nehemiah's refusal.

nehemiah-6:11:12.summary: Same intimidation campaign: enemies “frightening us,” and Nehemiah's resolve to strengthen his hands.
nehemiah-6:11:12.why: Ties the temple ploy to the broader campaign.

nehemiah-6:11:13.summary: David “placed his soul in his hand,” risking his life, a loose parallel of courage.

nehemiah-6:11:14.summary: Discouraging Israel from entering the land is unrelated to entering the temple to save one's life.

nehemiah-6:11:15.summary: Nehemiah's earlier refusal to “come down” lest the work stop matches his refusal here in the same chapter.
nehemiah-6:11:15.why: Shows a consistent pattern of refusal.

nehemiah-6:11:16.summary: “The one fleeing” from flame in an oracle on Assyria is unrelated.

nehemiah-6:11:17.summary: Believers scattered by persecution has no specific link to this verse.

nehemiah-6:12:0.summary: False prophets who strengthen the lawless broadly fit a prophecy given against God's servant.

nehemiah-6:12:1.summary: A qualification of overseers, “not a lover of money,” does not specifically connect to a hired prophet.

nehemiah-6:12:2.summary: Overseers “not greedy for shameful gain” is unrelated beyond a general money theme.

nehemiah-6:12:3.summary: Shepherds serving “not for shameful gain” is unrelated beyond a general money theme.

nehemiah-6:12:4.summary: A list of Babylon's merchandise has no link to a hired prophet.

nehemiah-6:12:5.summary: The Lord says of false prophets “I did not send them,” matching “God had not sent him.”

nehemiah-6:12:6.summary: Prophets who “divined for silver” parallel a prophet hired to speak against Nehemiah.
nehemiah-6:12:6.why: Same corruption of prophecy for pay.

nehemiah-6:12:7.summary: “The Lord has not sent you” to Hananiah matches “God had not sent him.”
nehemiah-6:12:7.why: Close verbal echo exposing a false prophet.

nehemiah-6:12:8.summary: Paul coveting no silver is unrelated to a hired prophet beyond a money theme.

nehemiah-6:12:9.summary: The spiritual person who discerns all things loosely parallels Nehemiah recognizing the false prophecy.

nehemiah-6:12:10.summary: Prophets profaning God for “a handful of barley” parallel prophecy bought with payment.

nehemiah-6:12:11.summary: Shameless, greedy leaders loosely parallel prophets serving for hire.

nehemiah-6:12:12.summary: Prophets who prophesy false things in God's name broadly parallel Semei's false word.

nehemiah-6:12:13.summary: The gift of “discernments of spirits” loosely parallels Nehemiah recognizing a false prophet.

nehemiah-6:12:14.summary: “A false vision” and “vain divinations” broadly parallel the false prophecy.

nehemiah-6:12:15.summary: Teachers exploiting in greed with “fabricated words” loosely fit a hired false prophecy.

nehemiah-6:12:16.summary: Prophets who speak “from their own heart and not from the Lord's mouth” match a prophecy God had not sent.
nehemiah-6:12:16.why: Clarifies what makes a prophecy false.

nehemiah-6:12:17.summary: Testing whether spirits are “from God” parallels Nehemiah recognizing God had not sent the prophet.

nehemiah-6:13:0.summary: Enemies gather with “reproach,” hoping Jeremiah will be deceived so they can prevail, like Nehemiah's foes.
nehemiah-6:13:0.why: Parallel plot to trap a servant of God.

nehemiah-6:13:1.summary: A general definition of sin of omission has no specific link here.

nehemiah-6:13:2.summary: Cutting off opponents' opportunity loosely parallels Nehemiah denying enemies grounds for reproach.
nehemiah-6:13:2.why: General theme of denying critics a pretext.

nehemiah-6:13:3.summary: God gives a spirit not of cowardice, a general contrast to the fear the enemies sought.

nehemiah-6:13:4.summary: Same campaign: the enemies' false report of revolt, another attempt to discredit Nehemiah.

nehemiah-6:13:5.summary: Preparing “a net” before a friend loosely parallels the trap laid for Nehemiah.

nehemiah-6:13:6.summary: Giving the opponent “no opportunity for abuse” loosely parallels avoiding a bad name.

nehemiah-6:13:7.summary: A question about whom one fears is only broadly related to being made afraid.

nehemiah-6:13:8.summary: Opponents devise a design against Jeremiah to “strike him with the tongue,” like plots to discredit Nehemiah.
nehemiah-6:13:8.why: Parallel scheme to discredit a servant.

nehemiah-6:13:9.summary: The Pharisees seek to trap Jesus, a general parallel to enemies trying to entrap Nehemiah.

nehemiah-6:13:10.summary: “Do not fear those who kill the body” broadly addresses fear of threats.

nehemiah-6:13:11.summary: The fate of “the cowardly” in the lake of fire has no specific link here.

nehemiah-6:13:12.summary: Seeking false testimony against Jesus loosely parallels hiring men to discredit Nehemiah.

nehemiah-6:13:13.summary: False witnesses set up against Stephen loosely parallel hired accusers.
nehemiah-6:13:13.why: General theme of hired false witness.

nehemiah-6:13:14.summary: “Do not fear people's reproach” addresses the very fear and “reproach” enemies intended.
nehemiah-6:13:14.why: Direct answer to intimidation by reproach.

nehemiah-6:13:15.summary: The value of a good name loosely relates to the threat of a “bad name.”

nehemiah-6:13:16.summary: “Do not fear them” is general encouragement against fear.

nehemiah-6:13:17.summary: Fearing mortal oppressors is a general parallel to the fear enemies sought to cause.

nehemiah-6:13:18.summary: “Do not fear their words” is general encouragement for a prophet facing hostility.

nehemiah-6:13:19.summary: Shown text condemns prophetesses who prophesy “from their own heart” for payment; only a general false-prophet parallel (truncated).
nehemiah-6:13:19.why: Background on false prophets for hire.

nehemiah-6:13:20.summary: Conduct that leaves opponents “nothing bad to say” loosely parallels avoiding a “bad name.”

nehemiah-6:13:21.summary: The worth of a good “name” loosely relates to the threat of a bad name.

nehemiah-6:13:22.summary: Daniel's rivals seek a “sin” to accuse him with and set a trap, like Nehemiah's enemies.
nehemiah-6:13:22.why: Parallel plot to provoke a fault to accuse.

nehemiah-6:14:1.summary: Paul leaves an opponent to the Lord, who “will repay him according to his works,” like “according to these deeds.”
nehemiah-6:14:1.why: Parallel of entrusting opponents to God.

nehemiah-6:14:2.summary: Jeremiah asks God to “remember” and judge those plotting against him.

nehemiah-6:14:3.summary: Priest and prophet going to an unknown land is unrelated to Noadia and the frightening prophets.

nehemiah-6:14:4.summary: Nehemiah's earlier prayer asks God to turn the enemies' reproach back on them, a similar imprecation.
nehemiah-6:14:4.why: Same speaker's pattern of prayer against foes.

nehemiah-6:14:5.summary: A plea against the arrogant and the fall of the lawless broadly parallels asking God to judge enemies.

nehemiah-6:14:6.summary: Judgment on prophets God did not send broadly parallels Nehemiah's prayer against the prophets.
nehemiah-6:14:6.why: General theme of false prophets judged.

nehemiah-6:14:7.summary: False prophets who lead astray is a general parallel.

nehemiah-6:14:8.summary: The psalmist prays against those who hid traps and schemed against him, a general parallel (truncated).

nehemiah-6:14:9.summary: Instruction on praying for a sinning brother has no specific link here.

nehemiah-6:14:10.summary: Longing for God in a desert land is unrelated to this prayer.

nehemiah-6:14:11.summary: Lying spirits in the mouth of prophets broadly parallels prophets used against God's servant.

nehemiah-6:14:12.summary: Introduces Hananiah, a named false prophet, broadly parallel to Noadia.
nehemiah-6:14:12.why: Example of a named false prophet.

nehemiah-6:14:13.summary: Judgment on “the false prophet” is a broad parallel only.
nehemiah-6:14:13.why: General theme of false prophets judged.

nehemiah-6:14:14.summary: Exposure of Hananiah as not sent by God is a general false-prophet parallel to this verse.

nehemiah-6:14:15.summary: Warning against false prophets is a general parallel.

nehemiah-6:14:16.summary: Many false prophets arising is a general parallel.

nehemiah-6:14:17.summary: Nehemiah's matching prayer “Remember me... God” shows the same remember-formula, here for good.

nehemiah-6:14:18.summary: Jeremiah seeks God's vengeance on men who seek his life, a general imprecatory parallel.

nehemiah-6:14:19.summary: Opponents of Moses and the truth broadly parallel opponents of Nehemiah.

nehemiah-6:14:20.summary: “The prophet teaching lawless things” broadly parallels the corrupt prophets.

nehemiah-6:14:21.summary: Prophets and prophesying daughters who speak from their own heart broadly parallel Noadia and the prophets.

nehemiah-6:14:22.summary: Hananiah smashing Jeremiah's collars has no specific link beyond false prophecy in general.

nehemiah-6:14:23.summary: A cry of abandonment is unrelated to this imprecatory prayer.

nehemiah-6:15:0.summary: Sanaballat hears of the same wall-building and mocks it; this verse records the wall's completion.
nehemiah-6:15:0.why: Frames the wall project from start to finish.

nehemiah-6:15:1.summary: The prospering righteous tree is unrelated to the dated completion of the wall.

nehemiah-6:15:2.summary: A promise to “build Jerusalem” broadly relates to completing Jerusalem's wall.

nehemiah-6:15:3.summary: The temple is “completed” with a dated month notice, paralleling the dated completion of the wall.
nehemiah-6:15:3.why: Parallel completion notice in the restoration.

nehemiah-6:15:4.summary: Sirach praises Nehemiah, “who raised our fallen walls,” the same achievement.
nehemiah-6:15:4.why: Later remembrance of this very work.

nehemiah-6:16:0.summary: The nations recognize “the Lord has done great things,” as enemies recognize the work was by God.

nehemiah-6:16:1.summary: When enemy kings “heard” of God's act their minds melted, like the nations' fear here.
nehemiah-6:16:1.why: Same pattern of hearing and dread.

nehemiah-6:16:3.summary: Sanaballat “heard” of the building and was angry, the same enemies hearing of the same wall.
nehemiah-6:16:3.why: Contrasts early mockery with final fear.

nehemiah-6:16:4.summary: Sanaballat and Tobia “heard” and were displeased, the same enemies at the project's start.
nehemiah-6:16:4.why: Shows the arc of the enemies' reaction.

nehemiah-6:16:5.summary: A work of merely human origin will fail, loosely contrasting with a work accomplished by God.
nehemiah-6:16:5.why: General theme of God's work prevailing.

nehemiah-6:16:6.summary: Declaring “what God will accomplish” broadly parallels recognizing the work was done by God.

nehemiah-6:16:7.summary: Enemies recognize “the Lord is fighting for them,” broadly like the nations' recognition here.
nehemiah-6:16:7.why: General theme of enemies acknowledging God.

nehemiah-6:16:8.summary: The same enemies “heard that I had built the wall,” the same event from earlier in the chapter.
nehemiah-6:16:8.why: Ties the enemies' fear to the finished wall.

nehemiah-6:17:0.summary: A high priest's family married into Sanaballat's, a parallel to Judah's elite tied to the enemy Tobia.
nehemiah-6:17:0.why: Shows enemy alliances reaching Judah's leaders.

nehemiah-6:17:1.summary: Shown text laments that no one acts rightly and friends cannot be trusted; only a general parallel (truncated).

nehemiah-6:17:2.summary: Betrayal and growing lawlessness is only loosely related to nobles corresponding with Tobia.
nehemiah-6:17:2.why: Only a broad theme of disloyalty.

nehemiah-6:17:3.summary: Nehemiah contends with the same “honored men” of Judah, though over a different matter.

nehemiah-6:17:4.summary: The leading men (“adoreem”) of Tekoa refused to serve in the work, a loose parallel to disloyal nobles.

nehemiah-6:18:0.summary: Lists “the sons of Era,” possibly the clan of Sechenia son of Erae, though the spelling differs.

nehemiah-6:18:1.summary: Lists “the sons of Era,” possibly the clan of Sechenia son of Erae, though the spelling differs.

nehemiah-6:18:2.summary: Names “Mesoulam son of Barchia,” the same man whose daughter married Tobia's son.
nehemiah-6:18:2.why: Shows Tobia's in-law was a wall builder.

nehemiah-6:18:3.summary: Names Mosollam son of Barachias, the same father-in-law of Tobia's son.
nehemiah-6:18:3.why: Identifies a builder tied to Tobia by marriage.

nehemiah-6:19:0.summary: The world's hatred of God's servants is only a general parallel to Tobia's hostility.

nehemiah-6:19:1.summary: Authorities threaten the apostles to stop their work, broadly like letters sent to frighten.

nehemiah-6:19:2.summary: A proverb on those who abandon the law praising impiety has no specific link to this verse.

nehemiah-6:19:3.summary: Same campaign: enemies “frightening us” to stop the work.
nehemiah-6:19:3.why: Links Tobia's letters to the wider intimidation.

nehemiah-6:19:4.summary: The Assyrian sends a message to undermine Hezekiah's trust, and Hezekiah receives the document; letters used to intimidate.
nehemiah-6:19:4.why: Parallel use of letters to frighten.

nehemiah-6:19:5.summary: Those who speak from the world is unrelated to Tobia's informants.

nehemiah-6:19:6.summary: The same aim that Nehemiah “might be afraid” appears in the hired prophet's scheme.

nehemiah-6:19:7.summary: The world hating Jesus has no specific link to Tobia's letters.

nehemiah-6:2:2.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
nehemiah-6:2:2.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

nehemiah-7:1:1.summary: Records the wall's completion, the event this verse resumes from.

nehemiah-7:1:2.summary: Hezekiah organizes priests and Levites to serve at the gates, a loose parallel to appointing Levites.

nehemiah-7:1:3.summary: Levites are set over the work after the return, a general parallel to appointing Levites.

nehemiah-7:1:4.summary: Lists priests, Levites and others living in Jerusalem, a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:1:5.summary: The builders “set up its doors” on the gates, the same doors Nehemiah now installs (truncated).
nehemiah-7:1:5.why: Same construction work on the gates.

nehemiah-7:1:6.summary: Levites appointed to sing and praise broadly relate to the appointment of singers and Levites.

nehemiah-7:1:7.summary: David's organization of Levites, gatekeepers and singers broadly parallels these appointments (truncated).

nehemiah-7:1:8.summary: Names “gatekeepers and singers” serving the house of God, the same personnel appointed here.

nehemiah-7:1:9.summary: David appoints singers for temple service, a general parallel (truncated).

nehemiah-7:1:10.summary: Sirach recalls Nehemiah who “set up gates and bars,” the same work.

nehemiah-7:2:0.summary: Choosing the faithful to serve broadly parallels appointing a trustworthy man.

nehemiah-7:2:2.summary: A faithful servant set over many things is a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:2:3.summary: An Anania in the covenant list is not shown to be the same man.

nehemiah-7:2:4.summary: The shown text about timber for gates does not mention the “bira” or its ruler.

nehemiah-7:2:5.summary: Faithfulness in small and large things is a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:2:6.summary: Obadiah the steward “feared the Lord greatly,” like Anania who “feared God more than many.”

nehemiah-7:2:7.summary: Reverence toward the Lord as treasure is a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:2:8.summary: Moses faithful in God's house is a general parallel of trustworthy service.

nehemiah-7:2:9.summary: Stewards must be “found faithful,” a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:2:11.summary: Mention of “the fear of God” is only a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:2:12.summary: Job is described as “true” and “God-fearing,” the same pair of virtues credited to Anania.

nehemiah-7:2:13.summary: Obadiah's claim to have feared the Lord is a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:2:14.summary: Daniel, faultless, is appointed over the kingdom; a loose parallel of appointing a trustworthy man.

nehemiah-7:2:15.summary: Nehemiah again appoints men “considered trustworthy” to a charge.

nehemiah-7:2:16.summary: Nehemiah acts rightly “because of the fear of God,” the same value applied to himself.

nehemiah-7:2:17.summary: Joseph's statement “I fear God” is a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:2:18.summary: Entrusting matters to faithful people is a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:2:19.summary: A faithful servant appointed over a household is a general parallel.

nehemiah-7:3:0.summary: Sheep among wolves and prudence has no specific link to gate regulations.

nehemiah-7:3:2.summary: Builders repaired “each opposite his house,” matching guards posted “each opposite his house.”

nehemiah-7:3:3.summary: Builders repaired “opposite their house,” matching guard posts opposite one's house.

nehemiah-7:3:4.summary: Unless the Lord guards a city “the watchman has kept awake in vain,” broadly fitting the setting of guards.

nehemiah-7:4:0.summary: Seeking God's kingdom first is unrelated to a sparsely populated city.

nehemiah-7:4:1.summary: Rebuilding ancient deserted places broadly relates to an unbuilt, underpopulated Jerusalem.

nehemiah-7:4:2.summary: Haggai rebukes people living in fine houses while God's house lies waste; here no houses had yet been built.

nehemiah-7:5:0.summary: Attributing one's sufficiency to God loosely parallels “God put it into my heart.”

nehemiah-7:5:1.summary: Crediting labor to God's grace loosely parallels Nehemiah crediting God for his plan.

nehemiah-7:5:2.summary: Another of Nehemiah's prayers, but it does not touch the census or God's prompting.

nehemiah-7:5:3.summary: “All Israel is recorded by enrollment in the book,” a parallel genealogical record of returnees (truncated).

nehemiah-7:5:4.summary: God “put” diligence “in Titus' heart,” the same expression for God prompting a leader.

nehemiah-7:5:5.summary: A warning not to be led astray has no link to this verse.

nehemiah-7:5:6.summary: Nehemiah's prayer against his enemies has no link to the census initiative.

nehemiah-7:5:7.summary: Laboring by God's working within is a general parallel to divine prompting.

nehemiah-7:5:8.summary: Refers back to “their record of the company,” the same register found here.

nehemiah-7:5:9.summary: Ezra's parallel list mentions those who “sought their record,” the same register of returnees.
nehemiah-7:5:9.why: Parallel account of the same list.

nehemiah-7:5:10.summary: God “put it thus in the king's heart,” the same idiom of God prompting action.
nehemiah-7:5:10.why: Same idiom of God moving the heart.

nehemiah-7:5:11.summary: God working in believers “to will and to work” broadly parallels God putting a plan in Nehemiah's heart.

nehemiah-7:6:1.summary: A report on temple building in Judea does not touch the list of returnees from deportation.

nehemiah-7:6:2.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's siege and capture of Jerusalem is the deportation from which these returned (truncated).

nehemiah-7:6:3.summary: Nebuchadnezzar besieges and breaches Jerusalem, the deportation behind this return (truncated).

nehemiah-7:6:4.summary: Nabouzardan removes the rest of the people to Babylon, part of the same deportation.

nehemiah-7:6:5.summary: The king of Babylon deports Jerusalem's people to Babylon, the deportation named here.

nehemiah-7:6:6.summary: A scroll found in Media is unrelated to the list of returnees.

nehemiah-7:6:7.summary: Shown text covers Judah's last kings before the exile; the deportation itself is not in the shown portion (truncated).

nehemiah-7:7:1.summary: Joshua the high priest, the returnee leader named “Jesus” in this list.

nehemiah-7:7:2.summary: Names Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest, the same leaders listed here.

nehemiah-7:7:3.summary: Refers to priests “in the days of Jesus,” the same high priest who led the return.

nehemiah-7:7:4.summary: Ezekiel's description of the creatures' wings has no link to the list.

nehemiah-7:7:5.summary: Zerubbabel appears in the line of descent after the deportation to Babylon.
nehemiah-7:7:5.why: Places Zorobabel in the Messiah's genealogy.

nehemiah-7:7:6.summary: Lists those who “came up with Zorobabel son of Salathiel and Jesus,” the same returning group.

nehemiah-7:7:7.summary: Gives the descendants of Jesus, the high priest named here.

nehemiah-7:7:8.summary: Nehemiah before the king is not shown to be the Neemias of this earlier list.

nehemiah-7:7:9.summary: Zorobabel and Iesous lead the returnees in starting the temple work.

nehemiah-7:7:10.summary: A lone name, Sechenia, does not match anyone in this list.

nehemiah-7:7:11.summary: Zorobabel and Iesous begin building the house of God in Jerusalem.

nehemiah-7:8:0.summary: The shown names do not include Phoros.

nehemiah-7:8:1.summary: Names members “from the sons of Phoros” returning with Ezra.

nehemiah-7:8:3.summary: Phoros heads the list of the people's rulers who sealed the covenant.
nehemiah-7:8:3.why: Same clan in the covenant list.

nehemiah-7:9:1.summary: Names members “from the sons of Saphatia” returning with Ezra.
nehemiah-7:9:1.why: Same clan in a later return.

nehemiah-7:10:1.summary: “Sechenia son of Erae” may belong to the clan of Era, though the spelling differs.

nehemiah-7:11:1.summary: The men beside Esdras do not include Phaathmoab.

nehemiah-7:11:2.summary: Phaathmoab appears among the rulers of the people in the covenant list.

nehemiah-7:12:0.summary: Names those “from the sons of Elam,” the same clan spelled Ailam here.
